The investigation focuses on measuring the mean B^0_s and B^0 meson lifetimes at the LHCb experiment using 9 nb^-1 of 2017 data. Our achievement involves applying improved signal selection criteria and enhanced fitting techniques to previous methods. Our current estimates for the mean B^0_s and B^0 lifetimes are 1.501 ± 0.013 ps and 1.530 ± 0.014 ps, respectively. A precise measurement of the B^0_s /B^0 lifetime ratio is also determined to be 0.997 ± 0.014. These findings, with their associated uncertainties, contribute to a comprehensive study of the B meson sector that enables in-depth exploration of possible deviations from the Standard Model. Specifically, our research leverages advanced sensitivity to possible New Physics influences in rare B^0_s and B^0 transitions, notably through constraints on rare decay processes like b->d gamma and electron/muon flavor changing neutral currents. Moreover, our work complements ongoing and future efforts aimed at refining the measurement of these rare processes. As an example, our current limits on rare B^0_s → μ^+μ^- and B^0 → μ^+μ^- processes are 1.0×10^-7 and 1.7×10^-7, respectively, where our results for these latter processes are already among the most precise worldwide. As the statistical component of these research efforts continues to improve, variations in rare B meson decays could potentially reveal hints of New Physics in the future. To this end, we have developed an automated tool that enables effortless interpretation of our findings in the context of 34-dimensional flavor physics. This work was accomplished in collaboration with the LHCb experiment and involves key contributions from all members of the LHCb collaboration. In addition to the insights gained from our research, our findings also highlight the significance of addressing outstanding issues in current understanding of the B meson sector and the numerous opportunities existing and future experiments will have to advance our knowledge in this field. As an example, the planned LHCb upgrade will enhance the experiment's sensitivity to rare B^0_s and B^0 transitions by a factor of at least 5. Similarly, the CTBC at the Beijing Sinotrace Collider will possess comparable or better sensitivity to a significant number of rare B meson processes. Consequently, further exploration of rare B meson physics at the level of New Physics beyond the Standard Model will be crucial in the future.

This study examines a class of algebras that lie within the infinite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras, focusing on a specific subset called finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras. We establish two main theorems that characterize both the nilpotent and solvable algebras within this class, based on their dimension. The results demonstrate that an algebra is neither nilpotent nor solvable if its dimension exceeds two, indicating a direct contradiction to a prior statement made by Kraschei in 1960. Furthermore, we derive the structure of these algebras for dimensions one and two, demonstrating that they map to known algebras, including the 2-dimensional Zinbiel algebra, the Albert algebra, the Nil-algebra, and the commutative algebra. The research also delves into the relationship between finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras and another algebraic structure known as filigree algebras, establishing a straightforward correspondence between them. The research was initially published in the journal Sibirskaia Matematicheskaya, issue 20, in 2020, and was subsequently published in the journal Algebra and Logic, volume 59, issue 3, in 2021, with some additional material included. The current paper provides a comprehensive review of both publications. This paper introduces the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model to analyze count time series that exhibit nonlinear dynamics and sudden shifts in patterns over time. Our research extends the PARX model by using Truncated Gaussian Hidden Markov models to dynamically change parameters in response to changes in the underlying state. We then derive a variational expectation-maximization algorithm for estimating the TV-PARX model parameters and implement it using a stochastic variational gradient Descent algorithm to update model parameters. We also develop a variational expectation-maximization algorithm for making predictions using the TV-PARX model. Finally, we test the TV-PARX model on simulated and real-world datasets, comparing its performance to other models, and find it outperforms these comparisons in terms of mean absolute error. The TV-PARX model code has been made available online for the scientific community. 

A key component of the TV-PARX model involves estimating the underlying states that drive the changes in the model parameters. We believe this approach holds value for its own merit, even in isolation, as it provides a solution to a problem that remains an open question in the time series analysis community. The research demonstrates how state-driven models can effectively manage nonlinear and dynamic patterns, and it paves the way for extending these models to more complex scenarios, such as multi-scale models. The TV-PARX model also offers a unique framework for addressing structural changes within the framework of the Hidden Markov model, and it offers a promising solution to a problem that remains a significant challenge in the community. We develop a method that enables the learning of object features through deep learning, allowing these features to be modified to guide the robot towards performing specific tasks as seen in limited demonstrations. By combining the learned features with a reinforcement learning controller, we significantly improve performance by reducing the number of required demonstrations. Our system was successfully applied to tasks like grasping and sliding objects, exceeding human performance with as few as five demonstrations each. Moreover, by analyzing the feature changes during task execution, we gained valuable insights into the underlying dynamics, demonstrating feature evolution patterns that are both intuitive and align with established scientific understanding. Our code is available at: \url{https://github.com/steve-robot/learning-descriptors}.

We developed a new method for calculating the vertical aerosol optical depth (AOD) without the need to calibrate wide-field photometry, building upon previous research by Leinonen and Jordan (2012). This approach uses comparative measurements between a camera looking at the full sky and one focused on a small field of view, taking into account the difference in scattering intensity. We applied this approach to data from the Sun angle imager at the Barstow, California station and the solar camera at the Mauna Loa Observatory, both in Hawaii. These measurements were then compared with those from co-located radiometers using the same method, and we found them to be in agreement in terms of aerosol optical depth, with a mean difference of -0.01 ± 0.03 for the camera at Barstow and -0.02 ± 0.03 for the camera at Mauna Loa. However, we also discovered issues with both cameras' ability to accurately measure AOD under conditions of high solar zenith angle or when the sun is close to the horizon. Additionally, we found the Mauna Loa camera to be inconsistent in its measurements, likely due to its large aperture, and we suggest using the Barstow camera for this type of measurement. Lastly, we believe wide-field photometry can be a useful tool for monitoring aerosol levels, but it requires regular calibration to ensure its accuracy. If not properly maintained, even a well-calibrated instrument like the one at Barstow may become inaccurate over time. We conclude that wide-field photometry can determine vertical aerosol optical depth without the need for absolute calibration, but it must be carefully maintained and compared with other measurements. Moreover, we propose a new method for calculating the solar zenith angle from the shadow of a camera's self-contained light source, which we found to be a reliable alternative to using a pyranometer, especially in desert environments. Additionally, we present a new parameter, called the "aerosol reduction factor", which normalizes the difference in scattering intensity between a camera looking at the full sky and one focused on a small field of view, taking into account the difference in scattering intensity, and we found it to be 2.54 ± 0.04 for the Sun angle imager at the Barstow, California station and 2.36 ± 0.04 for the solar camera at the Mauna Loa Observatory, both in Hawaii. Projecting a 3D model onto an image isn't difficult when the scene is straightforward, but estimating object pose becomes increasingly challenging in complex environments. Recent research has made significant progress in projection generation by dividing projected points into distinct groups, each representing a projected feature from the 3D model. However, existing methods typically project all points of the 3D model without consideration for missing data in images, which can lead to inaccurate pose estimation. In contrast, our proposed method, called Project2Pose, tackles this issue by first identifying the 3D points that can be projected onto the image and prioritizing these points over those that project to missing data. Our method achieves this by constructing two separate graphs that work in tandem: one for projecting 3D points and another for estimating pose. Our experiments show that Project2Pose outperforms the current state-of-the-art approach by a significant margin for challenging indoor scenes and also demonstrates improved performance on outdoor scenes. Additionally, our method provides a data term that can be utilized within a bundle adjustment, thereby offering an alternative to Project2Pose that is more efficient but less accurate. Our code is available at https://github.com/kevin4891/Project2Pose.

Notably, this method enhances the representation of data when compared to models that solely rely on linear regression. We also derive these findings using a "direct method" by solving the Dirac equation with a given metric. Furthermore, we determine the exact solutions to the Dirac equation in the $R$-Minkowski spacetime and interpret these solutions in the context of particle physics. We close by discussing the distinction between this approach and "indirect methods" of deriving the Dirac equation in modified spacetime geometries. We also consider a scalar field in $R$-Minkowski spacetime and show that it leads to a Klein-Gordon equation with a cosmological constant, in addition to a potential barrier that prevents particles from escaping a finite spacetime region. We also examine if it could prevent the expansion of the universe by providing a finite target space region that is surrounded by a potential barrier. We further investigate if this model leads to a steady energy input from the vacuum, which could explain the observed energy density of the universe. We conclude by highlighting the differences between this model and the idea of an expanding universe. We also consider if it could be tested through the gravitational effects of scalar fields on the motion of particles in laboratory experiments. This study investigates how a surface seal is affected by a pressure reduction inside a cavity as it collides with a solid surface. To simplify the analysis, a two-dimensional surface seal was modeled as having a rectangular cross-section and zero thickness, undergoing large deformations. The model includes the pressure reduction within the cavity, which was represented by an acoustic fluid. The model was tested at various speeds, from low to high, by striking a solid surface. The results showed that the pressure reduction inside the cavity accelerates the seal's surface velocity and reduces the pressure on the seal's upper surface. However, at higher speeds, the pressure reduction enhances the formation of the seal's tail and slows down the velocity of the seal's front edge. The research also examined the seal's surface dynamics at different speed levels, which revealed that the pressure reduction accelerates the velocity of the seal's front edge before it strikes the solid surface, and decelerates the front edge's velocity after the collision. The results also demonstrated that the pressure reduction accelerates the velocity of the seal's tail edge before the collision, and slows it down after the collision. The pressure reduction was found to influence the velocity of the front and tail edges of the seal more significantly at higher speeds than at lower speeds. Research involving quantum dots in III-V semiconductors, coupled to acoustic cavities, is highly promising for solid-state quantum electronics. To realize coherent control, it's essential to understand drive-induced Rabi oscillations between the quantum states, which we've directly observed in a GaAs wirelightwave structure. By modifying the driving laser frequency, we've consistently repeated Rabi cycles, whose amplitude is affected by both the quantum state occupation and cavity phonon population. A model incorporating both classical and quantum components successfully explains our findings. Furthermore, we've demonstrated the capability to intentionally detune the system to primarily interact with a particular quantum state and coupled cavity phonons. This discovery, combined with the system's ability to support long-lived quantum coherences, makes it an intriguing platform for both classical electronics and quantum information processing. Moreover, our study reveals that precise coherent control is feasible, enabling us to shift the frequency of the largest amplitude Rabi oscillation from 1.49 to 1.63 GHz. This remarkable frequency agility is a critical advantage over other quantum systems based on resonant tunneling diodes and nitrogen-vacancy centers, and we believe it could be beneficial for various applications in quantum electronics, such as quantum simulators, routers, and phase switches. To take the system to the quantum limit, we've implemented a quantum driver with a low noise of approximately 0.13% and a large signal swing of 420 mV, which we've used to investigate the quantum dynamics of Rabi oscillations in both Lambault's and Michelson-type configurations. Additionally, we've observed extensive multiplexing capabilities, where we've successfully controlled up to 32 quantum dots per micron using a 500 $\mu$m long wire, and we've found that the system's coherence time can be as long as 10.6 ms at 1.5 K. To address the energy efficiency of the system, we've calculated the power consumption of the quantum driver, which we believe can be as low as 10 fJ per Rabi cycle, and we've also explored the cavity phonon dynamics, where we've observed phonon trapping in a 300 nm long cavity at 1.5 K, and we've used this knowledge to develop a quantum driver suitable for the system, which we've tested in both the time and frequency domains. For example, dividing the lattice into separate square and triangular components leads to non-trivial topology and spin liquid physics. We examine single-photon fueled coherent states generated via two distinct mechanisms: beam splitters and parametric amplifiers. The analysis involves analyzing the quantum properties of these states, specifically their success probabilities, average photon numbers, and entanglement. The results are demonstrated through numerical means using the 4-dimensional Hilbert space formed by two coupled modes. The research reveals that the success probabilities of these states are significantly influenced by the gain of both beam splitters and parametric amplifiers, whereas the average photon numbers exhibit distinct tendencies with respect to these devices, exhibiting oscillatory behavior for the former and steady-state increases for the latter. The findings can serve as a basis for the analysis and generation of these states in experimental settings utilizing both classical and quantum resources. We introduce a novel method for representing polymers, grounded in the principles of substructure distillation, to efficiently handle large datasets of complex molecules. This approach identifies the most informative aspects of a polymer, specifically those related to its terminal monomers and bond connections, and distills it into a simplified substructure. We have applied this method to significant improvements in several deep learning models for predicting the physical and chemical properties of polymers. Our results show substantial gains, with property prediction models achieving an average increase of 12% in R^2 score and 25% in MAE when compared to conventional approaches. Our work also includes the development of a new training procedure for conditional neural message passing, a state-of-the-art model for property prediction, which overcomes current scalability limitations by an order of magnitude. Our code has been made publicly available at https://github.com/Tran-Thanh-Nguyen/Polymeric.

Conversational systems like chatbots and virtual assistants require testing frameworks that can efficiently and effectively evaluate their performance. Automated testing frameworks are crucial for this task but are often hindered by their own limitations when interacting with user interfaces. To overcome this challenge, developers are turning to GUI automation tools that can interact with these interfaces but can themselves be difficult to test due to their complex and dynamic nature. Current strategies that combine GUI automation with testing frameworks that use acceptance testing styles fail to account for the unpredictability of these systems. To address this limitation, we present a design for a testing framework called VIRTUOUS that is specifically tailored to automate testing of conversational systems that have a graphical interface. VIRTUOUS identifies the challenges associated with system unpredictability and finds ways to address this issue through strategies such as ignoring non-critical interactions, differentiating important events from background noise, dealing with partial system crashes, and recovering from these crashes. The framework's approach is evaluated through an example application to demonstrate its feasibility. Moreover, VIRTUOUS is an open framework that developers can adapt for their own testing needs. The source code for VIRTUOUS is presented in an appendices section that follows this paper. To facilitate understanding of the framework's design, we also include a detailed explanation of its implementation alongside pseudocode that illustrates the underlying logic. We conclude this paper by highlighting the limitations of the current implementation and suggesting areas for further improvement. We also explore possible pathways for enhancing the framework in the future. To demonstrate the effectiveness of VIRTUOUS, we present the results of an experiment that compared the performance of VIRTUOUS with a randomly generated testing strategy as well as a commonly used testing approach called PEST. The results showed that VIRTUOUS outperformed both the random and PEST strategies in terms of both efficiency and accuracy when testing a conversational system that is capable of sending and receiving messages. We also observed that the PEST strategy struggled with systems that had a complex decision-making process, whereas VIRTUOUS was able to adapt to these systems more effectively. We acknowledge the limitations of the current implementation of VIRTUOUS, particularly its inability to handle multi-threaded conversations and its reliance on manual input for certain commands. We highlight potential solutions to these limitations in the future work section of this paper. We also emphasize the importance of further testing VIRTUOUS on a wider range of conversational systems to validate its effectiveness in these scenarios. These studies involve analyzing the weakest possible conic formulation (WPCF) for specific problems. In some cases, known natural formulations on exotic cones turn out to have high dimensions, which may not necessarily indicate lack of solvability, as they might be equivalent to natural extensions on non-exotic cones with unknown WPCF dimensions. A notable example includes problems on knapsack cones and polynomial cones, for which an earlier study found that no natural formulations existed with a specific dimension. However, the current research discovered both existing natural formulations on knapsack cones and polynomial cones with dimensions that match the known WPCF for certain problems, including approximately doubling the previous known WPCF dimension for a specific class of problems. These results also extend to various generalizations of these cone types. In addition, the study found that existing natural formulations on geometric cones, hypercube cones, and sum-of-squares cones have dimensions that approximately match the lowest possible according to the current understanding of WPCF. A critical issue in using generative adversarial networks (GANs) for MRI reconstruction is ensuring that the trained model performs well on unseen data, regardless of the source or scanning protocol of the training set. We investigated how variations in the training dataset affect a model's ability to generalize across different MRI datasets, specifically in reconstructing T2-weighted foot and ankle images. We used a state-of-the-art VGG-based GAN to evaluate several scenarios, varying the scalp MRI included in the training set and with/without brain inclusion. Our findings showed that a model trained on brain MRI data, without included scalp, provided the best performance in reconstructing foot and ankle images, according to both structural similarity and peak signal-to-noise ratio metrics. Additionally, our research highlighted the limitations of current GAN models in generalizing to foot and ankle MRI data when the training set includes scalp MRI data, along with various protocols and data combinations. We open-sourced our MRI reconstruction dataset to support future research in this area.

This paper introduces a framework for network-based multi-agent optimization issues and presents a decentralized algorithm to solve these problems. A general formulation of the framework issues has been derived, which includes certain well-known problems like average cost and consensus. A decentralized decision-making algorithm has been developed and we have also obtained the convergence rate of the algorithm using operator theory. Specifically, we have shown that under certain conditions, the algorithm achieves a linear convergence rate of one step per time period. Additionally, we have established a connection between the algorithm and a centralized gradient-based algorithm, which has a linear convergence rate of $\frac{1}{2}$ per time period, provided the graph is connected. The study also provides an adjustment to the algorithm for handling unconnected graphs, which has a linear convergence rate of one step per time period. The proposed algorithm and its variants can be applied to a wide range of issues and systems, including power systems, transportation systems, and the Internet. A significant application of the algorithm has been demonstrated on a microgrid system. We introduce a basic dynamical system model called Motivation Dynamics to explain how agents in network environments make decisions. Originally developed to study single-agent decision-making, the model has now been expanded to accommodate multiple agents through the inclusion of external influence terms. These additions enable us to investigate how agents' motivations intersect and influence each other. In the version for multiple agents, we can generate mechanisms for cooperation and, as a specific application, it enables us to investigate dynamical system rendezvous behaviors. In this context, rendezvous refers to the convergence of different agents' decision-making processes over time. Our multiple-agent model extends previous single-agent models, and our research on rendezvous behaviors offers a new perspective on the complex topic of convergence in dynamical systems. These findings contribute to our understanding of how motivations intersect and influence each other and, as a specific application, provide a system model for the convergence of different decision-making processes, which has implications for our understanding of cooperation in networks. These research outcomes can be applied to various real-world scenarios, such as those involving social networks. We believe our model has value even in its current form and presents a foundation for further model enhancements. Our research was motivated by the study of two specific real-world examples: the convergence of population distributions and the cooperation dynamics of drones. However, our general model is applicable to a wide range of scenarios involving the convergence of different decision-making processes. This connection was an unexpected discovery during our research, and it has the potential to contribute to our understanding of the optimal stopping problem from a dynamical system perspective. Our research focused on the actinide compound GdxCm(1-x)Sn3, examining its electrical and magnetic properties across the Gd to Cm composition range. To achieve a comprehensive understanding, we compared our data with existing studies on GdSn3, CmSn3, and lanthanum based compounds with a similar crystal structure. Notably, we discovered a significant increase in the magnetic moment per formula unit in Gd0.5Cm0.5Sn3 compared to pure GdSn3 or CmSn3 compounds. To further illustrate the peculiar behavior of this compound, we analyzed its electronic structure using theoretical models from the density functional theory. These models revealed that mixing Gd and Cm atoms results in a significant change in the electron density of states at the Fermi level, which we linked to the compound's ferromagnetic nature. Our findings also allowed us to compare our data with other lanthanide and actinide compounds that exhibit similar crystal structures and electronic properties. Furthermore, we observed that the mixing of Gd and Cm atoms leads to an increase in the magnetic moment per formula unit, which we believe is uncommon among lanthanide and actinide compounds. Our research has contributed to a deeper understanding of the interplay between electron correlation, spin-orbit interaction, and the crystal electric field in GdxCm(1-x)Sn3 compounds, which we believe will be valuable for other compounds with a similar crystal structure that exhibit exotic electronic and magnetic properties. Ultimately, our study has shown that the compound Gd0.5Cm0.5Sn3 has exceptional magnetic moment per formula unit, which we believe makes it highly suitable for advanced magnetic memory applications. Researchers have utilized the H1 data from deep inelastic scattering to investigate the interaction of charm and beauty quarks, which are then used to study the characteristics of gluons within hadrons. To achieve this, computations of heavy quark production, aided by perturbative QCD, are compared to empirical findings, and the consistency of these interactions is established in various scenarios of proton collisions. Furthermore, gluon distribution functions, which describe the presence of gluons within protons, are determined through fits of relevant data, including those involving scattering of charm and beauty quarks, which in turn shed light on the structure of hadrons. These findings have been incorporated into existing knowledge and show that the properties of gluons within protons are inescapably uncertain, yet the distribution of these gluons across a broad range of momentum scales can be made apparent. Additionally, precedence has been established for further investigation into beauty quark scattering that was not previously considered, which is now seen as crucial for a more comprehensive understanding of hadron structure. 

(Tune, 2020)

We examined the characteristics of galactic halos using X-ray observations from a space telescope. A specific analysis was performed on a large group of galaxies with low mass, showcasing how the distribution of X-ray emission correlates with their mass, independent of the distance between their centers. Furthermore, a comparison was made between the total mass of these galaxies, as determined through X-ray and optical measurements, and the mass that is actually visible. The research revealed that the mass that is visible fluctuates according to the same patterns as the distribution of X-ray emission, and both are influenced by the same forces that cause small, compact objects like stars to collide and merge. The study has implications for our understanding of the formation of the cosmos and its ultimate fate, and it also provides a basis for further examining the composition of these galaxies and their surroundings using other observational techniques. The data used in the research was collected over a period of thirteen years. The expected outcome of the study is a three-dimensional image of one of these galaxies, showing how the mass and density of the cosmos change with distance from the center of the galaxy. The research was funded by a national institute and several space agencies, and it has been accepted for publication in a prestigious astronomical journal. The technique used to analyze the data has been tested on simulated observations of galaxies and halos, and it has been found to be accurate even when the mass of the galaxies is very low. The researchers have also studied the limitations of the technique, and they plan to improve it by combining the data from the space telescope with other observations of the same galaxies. The study has also highlighted the importance of continuing the current space mission to ensure the availability of future data, and it has been found to be cost-effective, requiring less than a tenth of the annual budget of a major space agency to operate for a period of ten years. The necessary computer processing power to analyze the data can be provided by a cluster of computers with a total processing power of less than a hundredth of the processing power of the most powerful computer currently in use. The formation of T centre ensembles in diamond is made possible by high-temperature treatments and results in the alteration of diamond's optical spectrum. Whereas individual T centres have unique spectral features, the characteristic diffusion spectra of the ensembles have been little studied and hold significant potential for quantum technology applications. In this research, T centre ensemble spectra were investigated across various temperature ranges using photoluminescence spectroscopy. As temperatures increased from 500 to 950°C, the diffusion spectra evolved significantly, with the ensemble's optical range broadening substantially. Furthermore, distinct sub-ensemble spectra were detected in the intermediate temperature range (between 700°C to 800°C), indicating that T centre distribution varies with temperature. Finally, a proposal is made for using statistical models to interpret the results and make predictions about the formation of T centre ensembles. Despite the ensembles' complex nature, this study demonstrates the feasibility of recovering the T centre density and distribution from diffusion spectra. Moreover, a proposed framework could be applied to other solid-state quantum systems featuring spatial inhomogeneities. Ultimately, this research paves the way for the development of quantum technologies using T centre ensembles by addressing the limitations of using individual T centres and providing a method for recovering precise spectral features from ensemble diffusion spectra. Additionally, the findings of this study can be extended to a wide range of group II ions in diamond, other color centres in diamond, and silicon-based quantum systems, all of which exhibit diffusion phenomena on various length scales. Consequently, considering the wide-ranging applicability of these systems in quantum technologies, further research should prioritize investigating the interplay between the systems' physics and their material platforms rather than the specific materials used. To this end, a framework is proposed for studying the interplay of physics, chemistry, and materials science in these systems with a view to developing robust, reliable, and controllable quantum technologies. Finally, the potential of T centre ensembles in diamond is highlighted for enhancing single-photon emission rates in quantum optoelectronics. To this end, a proposal is made for modifying the T centre distribution in diamond through chemical vapour deposition methods that can directly control the distribution of defects while preventing desorption at high temperatures. As a result, a robust and reliable T centre ensemble with broadened optical spectra could be achieved, thereby enhancing single-photon emission rates and making diamond T centres an appealing option for quantum technologies. Deep learning-based object detection methods, represented by the success of Faster R-CNN and its variants, have become the standard in object detection practices. Within the field of robotics, object detection is a crucial capability, and researchers and practitioners are seeking to incorporate the benefits of deep learning into robotic systems. This study investigated the performance of five cutting-edge object detection algorithms, including Tornado, Tornado-2, CenterPoint, M2Detection, and PAA, on a robotic part detection dataset. The primary objective was to determine the object detection model that exhibits the highest accuracy in a robotic setting. Furthermore, a design for integrating a detection model into a mobile robotic system was presented, and the effectiveness of this framework was demonstrated through a case study of a robotic system equipped with a lidar sensor. The associated dataset and code for this research are available online. The findings highlight the importance of selecting the object detection algorithm and the physical placement of the computer that operates it, with considerations for heat management to ensure the robotic system functions reliably. The research presented has implications for the safe and efficient detection of objects in a wide range of industrial robotic settings. The paper investigates existence and classification of solutions for a broad class of elliptic systems of polynomial equations, written as P(es,sb)(D_u,f_v) = 0, within the context of smooth functions f and g. Our findings address this system when addressed on a bounded domain Ω, subject to boundary conditions δ_u and g_v, and where the domain Ω has a specific geometric characteristic. We also examine the case where the system is defined on an infinite-dimensional space, under specific growth and asymptotic conditions. The system in question can be generalized to include nonhomogeneous equations and those involving partial derivatives, and we establish these results under the assumption that the unknown functions u and v possess a specific relationship. Our study also explores the connection to the Chern-Weil theory and provides an overview of the Cauchy functional system. We have an explicit example of a system that can be applied to Grigori Perelman's original manuscripts. Moreover, our research provides an explanation for the failure of the Hamilton-Simon conjecture. Finally, we outline a method for extending these results to a broader class of systems, those involving smooth functions f and g, and with the unknown functions u and v satisfying a specific relationship, Δ_u(f_v) = 0, where (Ω, g) is a Riemannian manifold without boundary. This last system includes the one examined by Frank G. Duncan. We have an appendix that contains an estimate useful for system solutions and another appendix that explores the connection between the Chern-Weil theory and the Cauchy functional system. Moreover, we have an additional appendix that explains the application of these results to the Hamilton-Simon conjecture and another one that explains the failure of this conjecture. We establish concentration inequalities for independent Bernoulli random variables that have a significant sum, expressed as a multiple of a certain range. These variables are then shown to satisfy concentration bounds for a wide range of convex functions and polynomial forms, surpassing previous achievements. Our techniques are adaptable to various counting processes, including random graphs and percolation on graphs, and provide the desired concentration inequalities for these processes. As an application, we derive an independent bound for the size of the largest cluster in subcritical Bernoulli percolation, measured as a percentage of the total number of vertices. This cluster size can be determined independently without knowing the percolation threshold. As an additional application, we establish the occurrence of a unique large component in random graph processes, including the Erdős-Rényi random graph and random regular graphs, with component sizes determined by first reaching a size of n^(δ) where 0 < δ < 1. Our results also include the inclusion-exclusion principle for independent Bernoulli random variables that have a significant sum. Our concentration inequalities can be extended to accommodate occasional large variable values, and our percolation and graph process applications can be extended to have multiple types of variables. Our first percolation application uses a new branching process calculation that can be applied to random tree processes. Our random graph application utilizes a new way to apply the inclusion-exclusion principle, in addition to its use in the form of Kolipanitcher's theorem. Our current achievements were inspired by, and are significant improvements upon, previous results obtained by Pisier, Kahn-Kalai, and by Reichman and Schipper in the context of random graphs and percolation. Our publication also rectifies an error in the original proof of an important inequality found in the work of Pisier. The study focuses on quadratic fields, denoted as Q, and uses matrices representing symplectic transformations over Q. The system of invariants for Sp4(Q) can be divided into two categories: one comprised of Hermitian forms with a specific discriminant, and another consisting of a set of pairwise linear factors, along with an additional parameter determining the form's type (non-trivial, diagonal, or scalar). We further simplify the model to obtain an analytical expression for the expected outcome, enabling us to compare two different acceptance policies, although we note that this analysis comes with the caveat that altering any aspect of the model results in an absence of an optimal solution under the current criteria. This study examines how word embeddings' flaws affect predictions in stock price forecasting. By applying a deep learning approach, we develop a model that incorporates word embeddings in a recurrent neural network. We put our model through numerous tests using various datasets and different embedding techniques, but we encountered issues when using conventional methods, likely due to how they often incorrectly associate opposites as similar words. This problem is particularly problematic in financial text analysis and we present an alternative approach called the Cosine Opposite Similarity (COS) score to address this limitation. The COS score is successfully applied to forecast stock prices but further research is needed to explore its utility in other contexts. Our code is available online. We also contribute a new financial dataset to the community. We discovered that the most predictive words often include financial terms like company names, industry designations, and specific stock symbols, but we found that the model can be gullible to these words, as seen in an experiment where we manipulated the model's input by replacing a stock symbol with a different one. Notably, we found that our model effectively incorporated the context of opposite words, as seen when we substituted the word "expensive" with "cheap" in a sentence, but we also found issues with the model when dealing with seasonal data, as we had to employ additional techniques, such as data augmentation and incorporating time-based embeddings, to achieve satisfactory results. We established a baseline by comparing our model with a basic LSTM network, and we found that the increase in accuracy was minimal when increasing the embedding size from 8 to 512. We prove that our proposed algorithm converges to a stationary distribution of actions that are not dominated, provided the transition probabilities and reward functions change slowly enough. These findings have implications for interpreting recent research on network dynamics and provide a foundation for further study into more complex models. We also compared our results to a random connection change model proposed by Newman, which our data did not match. Additionally, we found that the fraction of infected individuals can be calculated as a weighted average of the probabilities of connection changes, with weights dependent on the current network configuration. We demonstrated this weight value can be set to zero when the network consists of isolated clusters, which we theorized could also be applicable to other final states of the model. This paper presents our findings in fitting probability density functions (PDFs) for the distribution of partons within protons using various scattering data, top quark pair production data, and jet production data, with a focus on explaining how scale-dependent evolution affects fitting techniques. Our research demonstrates that for a given set of data, there is only one solution for PDFs when measured at a specific scale, eliminating the need to reintroduce fitting PDFs at other scales that are not of interest for subsequent analyses. In practice, this means that PDFs should be fitted using data that is relevant to the same scale at which it will be applied, and that includes the scales inherent in DGLAP evolution equations. To validate this conclusion, we conducted fittings for PDFs at different scales, combining an initial scale of 1.64 GeV with scales of 50 GeV, 500 GeV, and 5000 GeV, and compared the results to those obtained using standard fitting methods. Our study revealed that scales as low as 50 GeV can be effectively handled using the Hessian matrix method, while larger scales require the use of minimal covariance matrices. We also tested the impact of DGLAP evolution on PDF fitting as well as the use of polarized PDFs, but our primary focus was on the former. Our PDF set, fitting code, and Polarized PDF set are available for public use. Our research is significant because it highlights the potential biases that can arise from fitting PDFs over too broad a range of scales, a pitfall that is becoming increasingly relevant as researchers continue to explore higher energy scales. Our findings are crucial for ensuring the accuracy of PDF fittings in current and future experiments. Our results can also be applied to neutrino PDFs, although we have not tested the latter due to the limited availability of polarized neutrino data. Our research provides guidelines for minimizing scale-dependent evolution in PDF fittings. We have made our PDF sets and code public, and we plan to update our code regularly to accommodate any future developments in PDF fittings. Our research aims to promote transparency in PDF fittings by highlighting the potential biases that can arise from fitting over too broad a range of scales. Our study is significant because it can be applied to polarized neutrino PDFs, although we have not tested the latter due to the limited availability of polarized neutrino data. Our code is designed to handle polarized PDF fittings as well, although our primary focus was on the former. Our research is a response to the increasing relevance of fitting over large scales

We introduce a variance reduction based experience replay (VRER) framework that decreases the statistical ground truth estimation variance when using replay data, thereby improving policy gradient estimation. The proposed framework can be applied to various reinforcement learning tasks and algorithms, including those that utilize multiple learning rates and priority experience replay. We demonstrate the benefits of our VRER framework through concrete implementations, showing that it can enhance policy gradient estimation when combining experiences from distinct phases or using priority replay. The proposed framework also leverages natural variance reduction properties it discovers in policy gradient estimates, which can be particularly useful when data is scarce, as it minimizes unnecessary sampling. Our results are further validated by comparisons to existing efficient experience replay methods. The proposed VRER framework and the discovered property are applicable to a wide range of policy gradient algorithms and variance reduction techniques, providing valuable findings for the community. We have publicly available code to support our methodology.

To achieve this, we drew upon our understanding of the interplay between policy gradient estimation and variance, as well as the data sampling process. The resulting VRER framework proved to be valuable not just for our initial application, but also with other experience replay strategies, including priority replay and changing learning rates during training, which we tested on both simple and complex scenarios. The most intriguing aspect of the variance reduction based experience replay framework was the unexpected variance reduction benefit it provided when combining experiences from different time points, which we initially assumed would result in increased variance instead. This unanticipated finding gave rise to a new experience replay strategy that we have made publicly available, which we hope will be useful for the community. The development of the variance reduction based experience replay framework was motivated by our efforts to address the limited data challenge that is prevalent in robotics training, which we tested using the HalfCheetah environment from the Gym reinforcement learning framework, but the resulting experience replay strategy can be applied to any scenario characterized by limited data. The variance reduction based experience replay framework has a straightforward implementation, which we have made publicly available along with the results of our tests and the code used to conduct them, with the aim of facilitating further development by the community. We present a novel numerical approach for solving the gravity problem in the context of N-body simulations, building upon the foundation established by Gravity-Limited Adaptive Mesh (GLAM). Our enhanced code, MG-GLAM, achieves significant performance enhancements for specific applications, outpacing the original GLAM code by a margin of ten to a hundred times, and surpassing established N-body codes by a thousandfold. MG-GLAM leverages a hybrid algorithm to resolve gravitational interactions on a non-uniform mesh, employing multigrid methods to address potential accuracy issues. We demonstrate the code's efficacy by conducting a range of tests, including settling problems, collapse simulations, and N-body encounters. Moreover, using MG-GLAM for an existing large-scale simulation, spanning thirty-one years and comprising half a billion particles, results in a computational speed-up of over a hundred times with the same computational resources. Our study shows that the code can be very efficient, but also highlights some limitations that could impact its broad adoption. Our findings suggest that the multigrid algorithm may not always produce reliable results in certain scenarios, and the code requires further optimization to operate effectively on modern multi-core processors. We have open-sourced MG-GLAM on GitHub, and encourage the scientific community to contribute to its development. Our research highlights some critical insights into the trade-offs between computational efficiency and numerical accuracy in the context of N-body simulations. Our code can be used with various operating systems, and we have also made available some sample simulations for download from the MG-GLAM website. Our study has important implications for the scientific community working on N-body simulations, and our code can be a valuable tool for a wide range of astrophysical applications, from the study of planet formation to galaxy evolution. Our team is open to collaboration opportunities, and we are planning to use MG-GLAM for future N-body simulations, spanning thousands of years and involving billions of particles. Our code has the potential to make a significant contribution to the field of computational astrophysics, and we believe it is an important step towards achieving greater computational efficiency in N-body simulations. Our code is also relevant to other fields working on the resolution of the gravity problem in the context of N-body simulations, and our research can be applied to various domains, from cosmology to material science. Our team is planning to use MG-GLAM for future research projects, and we are committed to making our code an open and community-driven initiative. Our code is an significant advancement in the field of computational astrophysics,

This achievement is made possible by developing a marked metric description for the type of surfaces we are studying, which provides a key to proving the uniqueness of SLE$_\kappa(\rho)$ for $\kappa\in(0,4]$ and establishing that it maps the upper half-plane to the family of imaginary surfaces. Furthermore, we establish the convergence of discrete random processes to SLE$_\kappa(\rho)$ under the condition that the associated discrete surfaces converge metrically to the upper half-plane in a specific manner. A notable instance of this convergence occurs when considering random walks on Cayley graphs of groups of isometries acting on the upper half-plane and showing that the liminf of the corresponding discrete surfaces is a random SLE$_2$ curve. This generalizes previous outcomes by Kerian, Miller and Sheffield as well as Miller and Sheffield. A notable result that can be derived from this outcome is that the universal outer level set process associated with random walks on Cayley graphs of groups of isometries acting on the upper half-plane at its critical point is precisely the same as the outer level set process associated with SLE$_2$. This outcome is significant as it offers a mathematical explanation for a notable outcome observed in the computations of Dhar, Majumdar and Scheidler. A notable aspect of this outcome is that it may be obtained without referring to the results of the WATERSHED OUT PROCESS OUT OF WHICH ROCKS BREAK APART model that the same group of authors previously established for a distinct group of isometries. We investigate the implications of ultralight dark matter (ULDM) that couples to neutrinos, where the mass of the dark matter particle is much smaller than the neutrino oscillation energy scales. We demonstrate that such interactions could have a significant impact on the neutrino sector, particularly affecting neutrino oscillation patterns and influencing neutrino properties within the ULDM Compton length. This effect can be observed in the neutrino sector's evolution, particularly during the early universe, and may result in the overproduction of neutrinos within the ULDM perturbation holes, which could be detectable through future cosmic microwave background experiments. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between ULDM and neutrinos within the context of the standard model, the simplest scalar singlet extension, and the minimal left-right symmetric model. We also present achievable sensitivity for future experiments aiming to detect neutrinos within the ULDM perturbation holes through future cosmic microwave background and 21cm distribution studies. We further outline the reach of these experiments in detecting neutrino oscillations driven by a 1 eV mass scale, which would indicate a failure of the light neutrino mass generation mechanism. We also consider the potential for direct detection of the interaction between neutrinos and ULDM, which could occur through the formation of bound states, known as solitons, and examine the feasibility of direct detection through fixed target neutrino experiments and the next generation of dark matter direct detection experiments. We also explore the potential for the creation of neutrino-driven phase transitions in the early universe, which could result in the formation of neutral heavy dark matter particles, which might be detectable through direct detection or the relic neutrino background. We also examine the potential for the creation of neutrino-driven domain walls in the early universe, which could result from the breaking of a global symmetry, leading to a domain wall problem. We also consider the scalar triplet extension of the standard model, where the ULDM mass is sensitive to the neutrino mass, which could be determined through oscillation-driven phase transitions in the early universe. We also examine the neutrino-driven bulge formation in the early universe, which could affect galaxy formation and which might be detectable through future galaxy surveys. We also consider the ULDM-driven generation of primordial black holes and oscillatons, which could affect the relic neutrino background and which might be detectable through future neutrino experiments. We also explore the potential for the creation of neutrino-driven topological defects in the early universe, which could result from the breaking of a global symmetry,

The nonlocal gravity theory is modified to create a constitutive relation for an anisotropic medium that varies with direction, and this new relation is compared to the original nonlocal gravity theory by using a specific type of anisotropic medium made up of concentric spherical layers. It is observed that the change in direction of the anisotropic medium's nonlocal properties causes a shift in position of inner layers, and this shift affects the gravitational field and the masses of the layers. Additionally, the distinction between the nonlocal and local masses of the layers is highlighted, and these masses are found to be anisotropically distributed within the medium. The rates of mass loss of the layers also differ when there is a change in the nonlocal scale, and the nonlocal gravitational force is found to be anisotropically directed and its strength depends on the distance from the center of the layers. The implications of these findings on planetary bodies are discussed along with the suggestion that the Earth could be used as a test field for nonlocal gravity. The method of obtaining the constitutive relation is then explained for the benefit of those already familiar with nonlocal gravity. The relation is found to be similar to that derived using the post-Newtonian approach but with some differences, particularly when considering the levels of precision required for certain applications. The assumption of a small nonlocal scale compared to the size of the system being studied is also found to be necessary for the constancy of mass within that system over time. The discussion then turns to the topic of testing nonlocal gravity using planetary bodies before concluding with the idea that nonlocal gravity could be the mechanism behind the missing mass problem. The paper ends by highlighting the need for a more advanced mathematical approach to fully understand nonlocal gravity within the context of general relativity. The research described in the paper was conducted as a result of discussions held between the authors and V.L. Nakano. The paper represents a combination of two separate works: one on nonlocal gravity within the context of general relativity, and the other on the application of nonlocal gravity to planetary bodies. The original works were planned to be completed by the end of 2014, and the paper was finalized on January 12, 2015. The nonlocal scale used in the paper is based on a value of $10^{-4}$ meters, which is equivalent to about 20 times the radius of the Earth. The research described in the paper was supported by the National Science Foundation under grant number NSF PHY-08-51557

According to our findings, the impact of protein sequences is indeed substantial, with certain sequences influencing as much as 40% of relevant SNPs, even after considering other genetic factors. We also discovered varying levels of protein sequence influence across different traits such as blood characteristics, metabolic rates, and tendency to suffer from certain diseases. Furthermore, our study revealed specific patterns in protein sequences that are associated with certain traits, providing valuable insights into their functioning and potential manipulation through genetic modification. Our research discovered a significant increase in strange quarks within particles produced in high-energy proton-proton collisions that result in heavy-ion collisions.  Our findings show the phenomenon of strangeness enhancement at the Large Hadron Collider's lowest energy, and our calculations indicate that it is largely unaffected by an initial collision temperature change.  Compared to proton-proton collisions at the same energy, our data show an average 1.2 times increase in particle production that contains strange quarks in lead-lead collisions.  However, the production rates of these particles remain consistent with temperatures between 340 to 370 MeV. Furthermore, we demonstrate through numerical experiments that the introduction of an incentive mechanism can lead to an over-exploitation of easy tasks and, in turn, causes the system to become more unstable in the long run. To mitigate this effect, we propose a novel data-driven approach, the beta-dynamic task allocation (BDTA) method, which enables the system to adapt to changing distributions of task difficulties. We test the BDTA approach under various conditions and find that it consistently yields more stable and efficient outcomes compared to the baseline method, across different distributions of task difficulties. Notably, the proposed BDTA approach performs significantly better than the baseline method in scenarios with skewed task difficulty distributions, as well as in systems with large numbers of agents. We examine the connection between Pseudo Random Fourier Features (PRFF) and Random Fourier Features (RFF) within the context of approximating kernel methods, specifically focusing on the Gaussian kernel. It is demonstrated that PRFFs can be viewed as a refined version of RFFs, with a smaller feature space while achieving comparable performance. This advantage comes with a computational cost, as PRFFs require an additional training step to determine optimal centering parameters. We further investigate and analyze various applications of these feature approximation methods, including a detailed comparison of PRFF and RFF on synthetic and real datasets, showing that PRFFs generally provide better results at the expense of increased complexity. Moreover, we explore and validate the use of PRFFs and RFFs for nonlinear manifold learning and classification, respectively. The associated code has been made publicly available on GitHub. We create a theory of Cartesian Decomposition (CD) for subspaces under arbitrary group transformations. In particular, we develop this concept for Euclidean spaces, denoting it as Cartesian Decomposition (CD). A regular group action by a group of diagonal matrices is equivalent to a CD of the underlying space. Conversely, any CD defining a group action arises from just one compatible diagonal group. We call such a group the "determining" diagonal group associated with the CD. We establish that a diagonal group is the determining diagonal group for a CD if and only if it acts regularly on the underlying space. We further explore relationships between these determining diagonal groups and the algebraic structure of symmetric functions. We establish a connection between the ring of symmetric functions and the set of determining diagonal groups over a given set of variables. We name this ring the "diagonalizing" ring and denote it as D(σ). We discover that each element of D(σ) corresponds to a determining diagonal group and the map from elements of D(σ) to determining diagonal groups is an isomorphism of rings. We also find that any ring isomorphic to D(σ) corresponds to a determining diagonal group for some CD. We further develop the concept of a diagonal group being free from a set of subgroups, which we refer to as a "diagonalizing sequence". We discover that any diagonalizing sequence is equivalent to a CD of a Euclidean space. We establish that such a CD results in a group action by a group of polynomial matrices if and only if the sequence is finite. We also find connections between polynomial matrices and the ring of polynomials in symmetric functions. We name this ring the "polynomializing" ring and denote it as P(σ). We establish that P(σ) is a free ring with specific generators and relations. We discover that P(σ) is isomorphic to the ring formed by polynomial matrices acting on Euclidean spaces through Cartesian Decomposition. We also find that P(σ) is a free ring with specific generators and relations, which can be realized as a subring of the ring of polynomials over the rational numbers. We explore and describe the structure of this subring. We establish that any subring of P(σ) is isomorphic to a subring of the ring of polynomials over the rational numbers. This study examines the existence and nonexistence of compact conformally flat hypersurfaces in the Euclidean space of dimensions four and higher, with specific constraints on its scalar curvature and the norm of the conformal metric. We start by setting a lower bound on the scalar curvature, which enables us to prove the nonexistence of these surfaces for certain dimensions. Next, we establish an upper limit on the norm of the conformal metric, leading to a generalized Alexandrov-Ferran-Kazdan-Mineyev type result. Furthermore, we derive an inequality between the maximum scalar curvature and the square of the conformal factor, which in turn leads to a conclusion on the nonexistence of these surfaces for specific dimensions. We also obtain an estimate for the maximum scalar curvature, thereby establishing an relationship between the scalar curvature, the conformal factor, and the dimension of the space. This relationship enables us to extend and improve previous results by Geroshkovich, Kazdan-Mineyev, and Nelli, among others. We also address the case where the scalar curvature is upper-bounded, which results in the nonexistence of these surfaces for dimensions five and higher. A novel energy-efficient strategy called Generalized Antenna-Switching Technique (GAST) is proposed for a single-user, single-pair communication network with the ability to supply and consume power, enabling simultaneous data transmission and energy harvesting. The GAST can be applied over various frequency bands and protocols, and results in an significant increase in the achievable rate compared to other methods. The problem of maximizing rate subject to power constraints is then examined, and an optimal solution is obtained using convex optimization techniques. The resulting algorithm is then tested under real-world conditions, yielding outcomes that outperform other techniques in various scenarios. The outcomes reveal that the proposed method yields an approximately 1 order of magnitude increase in rate over time, and rate over time can be reduced by approximately 10 times. The proposed method is also found to be highly effective in overcoming other techniques in scenarios with low communication rates, and the appropriate parameters for switching between different frequency bands are then determined, yielding an approximately 50% boost in rate. The outcomes obtained under real-world conditions are then applied to a repeating scenario, yielding an approximately 20% boost in rate. The proposed method is also found to be robust, enabling the simultaneous transmission of data and the charging of a base station, and outcomes obtained under this scenario indicate that the base station can be fully charged within approximately 12 hours, and the appropriate parameters for switching between different frequency bands are also determined, yielding an approximately 25% boost in rate. The effectiveness of the proposed method is also validated through outcomes obtained in various scenarios with different numbers of frequency bands, and the appropriate parameters for switching between different frequency bands are also determined, enabling an approximately 20% boost in rate. Specifically, we investigated Northern Minden's 2009 model, which assigns a label to each node indicating how it reacts when removed from the network. These labels range from -1, signifying a node that always causes a cluster, to 2, denoting a node that only causes a cluster when it is the sole target for removal. Our primary goal was to analyze how the fragmentation of the network changes in response to removing any single node. We found that the average size of these node removal-induced avalanches can be significant, especially in networks where many nodes have a reaction label of 2. Our main discovery was that the size of these avalanches is directly proportional to the square root of the number of nodes in the network, regardless of its total degree. We demonstrated this proportionality through mathematical analysis and confirmed it through statistical means. Our research also revealed that the networks themselves are highly interconnected and cluster into large components that are themselves highly interconnected. We were unable to determine specific degree distributions from our generative model. We tested the resilience of these networks by removing one node at a time and found that they are not robust in this scenario, fragmenting completely in many cases. We introduce a novel metric interferometry system called sloshing-Sagnac interferometry and demonstrate how it surpasses the sensitivity of conventional meter-scale Sagnac interferometry by several orders of magnitude. This achievement is made possible by utilizing an extremely small illumination area in relation to the interferometer's size and combining illumination and measurement processes. A theoretical analysis of this configuration yields an signal-to-noise ratio that is directly proportional to the square of the meter-scale interferometer and is thus highly sensitive to minuscule changes. We further explore this idea's applications in a sloshing-Sagnac gravimeter and a variable meter-scale interferometer, discovering that it can match or exceed the sensitivity of state-of-the-art gravitational measurements, all while utilizing significantly simpler design components. We also examine the sloshing-Sagnac's ability to detect varying meters-scale interferometer lengths and find that it can achieve an incredible 10 fm resolution, a level of precision that has never been achieved before. We conclude by highlighting the vast potential of this innovative design, urging the scientific community to adopt and further develop this groundbreaking idea. This paper presents a new wireless protocol called NOVR-XL for next-generation XL-MIMO systems with massive connectivity needs. To enhance performance, the proposed protocol includes a new component called Prioritized Acknowledgement (PA). However, incorporating PA results in acknowledgment overhead increasing significantly, which could lead to a bottleneck. To mitigate this, we developed a new schedule called Semi-Static Acknowledgement (SSA) to minimize the impact. SSA achieves a balance between PA efficiency and acknowledgment delay. To further improve performance, we introduced a new model called NOVR-XL RA (Scheduling) to prioritize acknowledgments based on system performance. To evaluate the efficacy of these proposed components, we conducted simulations, which showed a significant improvement in performance. To accommodate even more connections, we explored extending the protocol to hybrid XL-MIMO systems. To further optimize the protocol, we investigated several alternatives for acknowledgment scheduling. To facilitate practical implementation, we developed an algorithm to determine optimal acknowledgment timing. To evaluate the proposed protocol in a realistic setting, we created a simulation environment that reflects actual wireless base station conditions. To explore the limits of the protocol, we analyzed its performance mathematically. To summarize, this research leads to several conclusions about the proposed protocol, including its ability to handle a high number of connections, its efficiency in reducing acknowledgment overhead, its ability to adapt to changing system conditions, and its scalability to hybrid XL-MIMO systems. To facilitate replication of the work, we made the simulation code publicly available. To the knowledge of the authors, this is the first wireless protocol ever to be both publicly available and generate the underlying research that led to it. To explore applications of the protocol, we considered several scenarios, including those with a high number of connections, varying acknowledgment delays, and different hybrid XL-MIMO system configurations. To evaluate the protocol in these scenarios, we used several performance metrics, including acknowledgment delay, throughput, and average system utility. To make the code useful to a broad audience, we included detailed documentation of the simulation setup and the algorithm used to schedule acknowledgments. To ensure integrity of the code, we used a code integrity verification tool. To facilitate extension of the code, we made the underlying MATLAB code available. A key challenge in understanding the evolution of protoplanetary disks lies in connecting substructures within these disks to planetesimals, and eventually planets. To address this, we developed a comprehensive model that incorporates both one-dimensional radiative hydrodynamic simulations and N-body N-particle disintegration dynamics models. This combined framework enables us to investigate the mass distribution of disintegrated substructures during gravitational instability, as well as the formation of planetesimals through various mechanisms such as gravitational perturbations, density waves, and gravitational streams. By applying this model to a specifically analyzed section of a protoplanetary disk, we found that large-scale substructures can produce planetesimals with a size spectrum, while smaller-scale substructures primarily create embedded particles around density waves, which, in turn, may give rise to gravitational streams. These results suggest that both long-lived massive accretion streams and pebble isolation layers could serve as potential sources of planetesimals, especially in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks. Furthermore, we discovered that the formation of planetesimals is heavily influenced by their orbital configuration, specifically their radial migration, and that the resulting planetesimals exhibit a size-dependent velocity dispersion, with smaller sizes exhibiting greater dispersion, despite being more susceptible to stickier agglomeration processes. These findings provide a basis for understanding the composition and evolution of planetesimals in a given substructure within a protoplanetary disk. To utilize this model at a disk-wide scale, we introduce the Planetesmal Formation Parameter Space, which encompasses a variety of substructure formation mechanisms, including both gravitational and aerodynamic processes. Ultimately, this research paves the way for an integrated model of protoplanetary disk evolution and planetesimal formation, as well as Planetesmal Formation Parameter Space modeling. To that end, we developed PPDModel, an open-source code that can be found here: https://github.com/PlanetesmalFormation/PPDModel. A nonlinear nonlinear nuclear matter equation of state is proposed to describe nuclear matter properties at finite densities. The approach involves a linear combination of the Levenberg-Marquardt and gradient descent methods for optimizing the parameters of the BigApple energy density functional. Utilizing the Dirac-Dirac choice for the single-particle wave functions, calculations were performed for even-even Sn isotopes and isotones to determine the ground-state energy minimization. The predicted equation of state for nuclear matter can be described by a polynomial fit in terms of density and pressure. The research indicates that the BAKASH II parameter set fails to reproduce the observed trends for certain isotopes, thereby necessitating a re-examination of that set. The derived nonlinear equation of state allows prediction of the equation of state for nuclear matter at the infinite level, which can be compared to existing models. Key features of the proposed equation of state include: (i) the success of the BigApple energy density functional is limited to a specific range of spin and isotope; (ii) the re-evaluation of the BAKASH II parameter set is advised; (iii) the proposed approach can be applied to other groups of nuclei by adjusting the relevant parameters. The work presented here contributes to the understanding of nuclear matter properties, specifically the equation of state at finite densities, and may have relevance to heavy-ion collision research, particularly LHC energies. The associated research was conducted as part of a Ph.D. thesis accredited by the University of Lund, Sweden. The studied nuclear matter properties can also be applied to neutron stars, which are linked to pulsar properties, and to finite nuclei properties, which are linked to isotopic chains. The related research was supported by the Swedish Nuclear 2010 programme, the Goran Gustafsson Foundation, the Royal Physiographic Society in Lund, the Magnus Bergvall and Christina Thrane Foundation, the Lund University Centre for Nuclear Physics, and the Nordic Nuclear Physics Programme. We investigate the performance of Molmer-Sorensen gates under frequency errors caused by laser mistuning, varying natural oscillators, or compensation via motional entanglement, within the framework of frequency robustness. A carefully tailored implementation of these gates, taking into consideration both duration and number of applications, demonstrates a significant increase in entanglement generation among trapped ions. This approach, combined with optimal duration optimization, results in a notable improvement in achieving high-fidelity entanglement, especially in large-scale systems. Our findings indicate that while overcast design does provide a degree of frequency tolerance, it is crucial to consider the specific frequency characteristics of individual trapped ions, averaging across all participants in a chain to achieve the highest possible robustness. Our study illustrates the relationship between gate design, frequency robustness, and the resulting distribution of entanglement, both among individual ions and within the overall chain. We establish the criteria for a well-entangled state and present the results of various experiments, including both single-qubit and two-qubit logic operations, demonstrating the feasibility of frequency-robust Molmer-Sorensen gates in actual trapped ion systems. Our proposed design has been successfully implemented on the Bigrain experimental platform, located at the CNR-IOM Trapani, Italy. Our research highlights the importance of balancing duration, number of applications, and 245 GHz frequency tuning to achieve balanced distribution of entanglement among trapped ions, ultimately leading to a higher success rate for logic operations following M\-S gate ensembles. Our findings also reveal the limitations of overcast design and the need to consider specific frequency characteristics of individual trapped ions to achieve frequency robustness, a trait that can be readily realized using state preparation duration manipulation and multiple application scaling. Our study paves the way for a general frequency robust standard for Molmer-Sorensen gates, providing a practical solution for large-scale trapped ion quantum computing systems, including both near-term intermediate-scale and large-scale quantum processors, such as AION1000. Our results are further highlighted by the recent trapped ion quantum processing unit intermediate-scale record achieved on the AION1000 platform, located at the CNR-IOM Trapani, Italy. Our frequency-robust Molmer-Sorensen gate design has been recognized as a top candidate for the IOP Publishing Quantum Science and Technology journal cover following its initial publication in 2022. Recently discovered gestermanite, GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$, is an uncommon solid state compound that possesses both Dirac electrons and strong many-body physics, making it an intriguing subject for scientific study. Born-Haber cycle calculations were used to investigate the formation reactions of this compound and a corresponding proxy compound, Cu$_{9}$Cl$_{9}$(OH)$_{36}$, which lacks the gallium content. These calculations showed that the compound's stability is supported by both strong covalent bonding within its atomic components and significant contributions from electron-electron interactions, which are indicative of strong many-body physics. Through comparison with proxy compound Cu$_{9}$Cl$_{9}$(OH)$_{36}$, it was found that gallium plays a crucial role in strengthening covalent bonding and reducing the compound's electron density, which is essential for its unique properties. Moreover, gestermanite's electronic structure can be modified by tuning the atomic components' covalent bonding, which may lead to an exciting combination of Dirac electrons and strong correlations and could be useful for designing materials with tailored electronic properties. Furthermore, this compound belongs to the family of alpha-layered oxides/hydroxides/chlorides, which has low interfacial energy and may have applications in designing heterostructure devices, catalyzing redox reactions, and supercapacitor electrodes. Theoretical calculations also predicted that gestermanite could be a versatile 2D anisotropic type-I van der Waals semiconductor with a indirect bandgap of 1.5 eV and could be transformed into an anisotropic metal by applying pressure. The predicted properties of this compound make it an attractive subject for experimental verification and possible utilization in various technological scenarios.
