To achieve this, we apply Griffiths' approach to analyzing the compactness of the K\"ahler cone, combined with the use of non-standard models of complex manifolds. Furthermore, our method enables us to investigate the connection between geometric and standard compactifications of abelian variety moduli spaces, with specific consideration given to those with maximal Hodge structure. To accomplish this, we draw upon Descent of Algebraic Structures, where Descent of Algebraic Structures delves into the topic of variational Hodge theory and the standard compactification of moduli spaces. Additionally, we touch on the subjects of abelian schemes and variation of Hodge structures within the framework presented. Lastly, we outline possible future directions for study, including but not limited to, the application of our method to Calabi-Yau and K3 surface moduli spaces.

This absence of low-mass stars is particularly evident in galaxies that are spatially compact and show a high velocity dispersion, likely as a result of interactions within galaxy clusters. Thanks to significant advances in NLP, models capable of capturing the intricacies of natural language have been created. These models are often effective when applied to tasks such as sentiment analysis, but they are generally biased towards the language they were trained on and require substantial data to be effective in other languages. Our research presents a multi-task model that is a variant of the multi-layer LSTM network and includes an attention-based mechanism to capture contextual information. When applied to sentiment analysis across different languages, our model achieves a 0.5% improvement on average in F1-score compared to the current standards. When applied to a different language on which it wasn't trained, our model shows a 10% F1-score improvement on the standard baseline. When applied to a larger language dataset, our model shows a 5% F F1-score improvement on the current baseline. Our model also achieves a 20% F1-score gain on the existing baseline when the task is to combine sentiment analysis with part-of-speech tagging. Our code is available online for the community to use.

As hospitals face an overwhelming influx of patients during the COVID-19 pandemic, it's becoming increasingly vital to prioritize those in need of critical care the most.  While early work focused on general patient allocation, our research proposes a novel approach tailored to intensive care units (ICUs).  We begin by identifying key features associated with ICU admissions, which we then use in a machine learning model to classify patients into low, medium, or high-risk categories for ICU admission.  These categories are tied to specific features such as blood oxygen levels, temperature, and the presence of particular conditions, which in turn are used in a decision tree to determine allocation to an ICU, regular ward, or home discharge.  When put through a simulation of varying hospital capacity and patient flow conditions, our model showed an 8% better success rate at meeting ICU admission demands than traditional methods, which is a 21% improvement when measuring mistreatment error.  Furthermore, our model also showed a 20% reduction in ICU bed occupancy and a 15% increase in overall patient survival rates.  At the same time, it only required 1 parameter to be set, which it achieved by minimizing the sum of the squared errors between actual and predicted ICU admission demands over time.  This model has the additional benefit of providing actionable data for healthcare staff and it can be applied to any hospital setting.  Which we demonstrate through an example based on real data from a specific hospital.  In short, our model offers a data-driven solution that can give better results than the methods currently used by hospitals. The paper develops the fundamentals of a category of simplicial groups under the Wright hierarchy, denoted by Omega(G)-groups, and demonstrates that this category is equivalent to the category of simplicial groups in Omega(G)-equivalences, thereby establishing an connection to the universal bundle functor for the Omega(G)-construction. It is further proven that the universal bundle functor over the Wright hierarchy corresponds to a natural transformation that forms a monad within the category of simplicial groups in Omega(G)-equivalences. In the process, the paper makes use of the principles of the simplicial group model for rational homotopy theory. It also includes an examination of the relationship between the simplicial group model and the category of omega-simplicial groups. Moreover, it provides a group-like structure to the omega-simplicial groups and the Wright hierarchy, thereby facilitating the incorporation of integral coefficients. Finally, it explores the properties of a particular class of omega-simplicial groups known as the Maschke omega-simplicial groups. It concludes by discussing an application to the study of rational homotopy types of spaces with gradient structures. It additionally outlines future directions for research, including the potential extension of the category of omega-groups to categories of groups with additional structure. It highlights the potential of this framework for incorporating integral coefficients and the possible implications for the Eilenberg-Moore spectral sequence. It also touches on the possible connections to the Milnor conduction theorem and the role of the Steenrod algebra in this context. It emphasizes the need for further investigation into the relationship between the omega-construction and the bar construction, as well as the development of a method to determine the rational homotopy types of spaces with gradient structures. It finally mentions the presence of preliminary versions of some of the paper's results in older studies. It also references the work of other notable mathematicians who have contributed to the field of rational homotopy theory, including Jean-Pierre Serre, Daniel Quillen, and Victor Gugenheim. Visual Relationship Detection aims to identify relationships between objects within images and has several applications in areas like traffic management. A major challenge in VRD is the imbalance in negative samples, which can be mitigated by proposing balanced samples. We examine two methods for sampling, including the standard Negative Proposal Sampling (NPS) and propose Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS). The BNPS strategy prioritizes the most uncertain predictions and focuses on proposed samples with low confidence scores. Our strategy achieves this balance without increasing the number of proposed samples. We put BNPS through testing on the Visual Relationship Detection dataset and the results show an improvement of 4.5% in mAP over the baseline method. Our code is available at this link https://github.com/zhongyurui/VRD-BNPS.

- Train the model as specified in train_model.ipynb. 

As for the dataset, you can download it from the following link: http://aiwu.org/VRD.

A significant X2 solar flare occurred on November 7th, 2004, alongside two massive filaments that reached heights of over 100,000 kilometers above the solar surface, forming one of the tallest hot plasmas ever observed. As the flare and associated eruptions emitted enormous amounts of energy, they created shockwaves that interacted with surrounding magnetic fields, resulting in extreme magnetic unstability on the lower solar atmosphere, closely resembling conditions found on the upper solar atmosphere. Utilizing data from multiple sources, researchers found that the flare's effects were confined to a very small area, with temperatures reaching 45 million degrees Celsius, and in-depth examination revealed how particles were accelerated to high energies, and the massive filaments' ability to reach great heights was facilitated by solar winds. Furthermore, they discovered that the flare's impact was global, with effects being felt on the lunar surface, and in the Earth's magnetic field, where it caused a 10% increase in solar wind. Moreover, the flare's energy release was so intense that it caused the lunar surface to heat up, and the Earth's magnetic field to strengthen, and even allowed the researchers to map the solar wind acceleration process that leads to the formation of solar flares, and to study the interaction between the flare's hot plasmas and lunar regolith. Additionally, the event provided valuable insights into the formation of solar corona, and the energy sources available for mass loss from the solar surface. The data collected from this event was sufficient to create a comprehensive model that can be applied to other solar flares of a similar nature, and it has been observed that such events occur about once a year during the solar maximum phase. KIC 9267654 is a solar-type star that was found to have unusual characteristics when first studied in 2011, featuring rapid rotation and strong solar-like oscillations. Additional research from high-resolution spectroscopy and long-term monitoring of the star's activity and oscillations are presented here. To determine the star's precise age, mass, and chemical composition, multiple techniques were employed, and the findings suggest it has a mass similar to the Sun, is somewhat younger than the Sun, and has a similar chemical composition. Previous hypotheses about the star's rapid rotation were likely incorrect, and new findings suggest that its rotation speed varies significantly between its equator and poles, a feature more commonly seen in younger stars. The discovery of a slow-spinning solid core in the habitable zone of KIC 9267654 makes this star an intriguing subject for studying unstable solar-like oscillations and core hybrid oscillations, and further study could provide valuable insights into its internal dynamics. The potential factors contributing to the star's unusual rotation profile are also discussed, including the possibility of it having a planetary companion that could have caused tidal forces leading to the formation of the core over time, and leading to a potential search for planetary orbits similar to that of KIC 9267654. Fake news has been a significant concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. To combat the spread of false information, detecting fake news is crucial, and deep learning techniques have been highly effective in this area. Our proposed approach, MetaFEND, leverages a meta-learning algorithm to enhance the detection of fake news by creating a framework that can be applied to various platforms, including Twitter. In the proposed scheme, a feature extractor learns to identify both semantic and temporal patterns specific to each dataset, while the classifier determines the authenticity of the text. To improve performance, a contrastive loss function is incorporated that compares real and fake news. Our model achieves the best results on both Twitter and FEVER datasets, outperforming the current state-of-the-art models in terms of accuracy, F1-score, and AUC-score. To facilitate the widespread use of our model, we provide a user-friendly API that can be integrated into various platforms. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/gholamhosseinmohammadi/MetaFEND.

These positions also determined either positive or negative exchange interactions, along with either gradual or sudden changes. These findings will help develop a silicon computer by identifying optimal placement of dopants and exchange gates.

A comprehensive assessment of this method has been conducted through a series of experiments, testing its capabilities on both solitary and combined lung lesions in the liver, and on pancreatic tumors in the abdominal region. The paper introduces Group Lasso, a variational inference algorithm for natural language processing, which reduces variables to the most significant words within part-of-speech tags or noun phrases. This algorithm achieves excellent results in various tasks, including part-of-speech tagging, noun phrase extraction, and semantic role labeling. As evidence, it delivers the best performance to date in the PTB sentence semantic labeling dataset, surpassing the previous record by 13.1% in F-score. Additionally, the paper presents a method to extend Group Lasso, called timed Group Lasso, which considers both word importance and temporal information, leading to an optimized solution for labeled temporal segmentation, previously unaddressed in the literature. This approach is applied to a dataset with complex temporal relationships, yielding a score of 85.6% in F-score, a significant improvement over the current baseline of 66.8%. The paper's contributions are further validated by substitute training and model selection experiments, yielding consistent results. In the first case, an unentangled atom is placed in the cavity, and we investigate how it affects the generation of two-atom entanglement between the resident atom and the trigger atom through cross-Kerr nonlinearity. This results in the creation of a Bell-state correlation between the two atoms, even when the cavity is initially unpopulated. In the second scenario, an unentangled atom is positioned in the cavity and interacts with a pre-existing Bell-state entanglement between the resident atom and a third atom through a classical control, leading to the creation of triangle entanglement among the three atoms. In both instances, the duration of interaction required to achieve maximal entanglement can be minimized by selecting an optimal initial coherent state in the cavity. Furthermore, the classical control phase can be adjusted to prioritize either two-atom entanglement or three-atom entanglement, thereby exerting control over the generation of multipartite entanglement. The potential of the cavity system is highlighted by the ability to generate triangle entanglement among three atoms in a few microseconds, which is several orders of magnitude faster than other proposals, and could be further enhanced by incorporating a superconducting quantum interconnect bus based on cavity QED. The robustness of the scheme is demonstrated by the insensitivity of the results to photon decay within the interaction period. Social media feedback from customers contains valuable information that can be utilized by businesses to better understand their customers' sentiments. This study leverages LSTM networks to classify Twitter user sentiments based on their comments. Our approach involves using a dataset of 32000 Twitter comments, spanning 10 distinct product categories, to train a deep learning model. We conducted a series of experiments utilizing Conv-LSTM networks and hybrid models that combine LSTM and Conv-LSTM layers to classify the Twitter comments. Our findings reveal that the LSTM network performs the best, achieving an f1-score of 0.78 in the Apple product category with the lowest f1-score being 0.57 in HPC services. Furthermore, a comparative analysis is performed with a recurrent neural network to validate the effectiveness of LSTM networks in this application. We also examine the hybrid model's performance and find it to be inferior to the LSTM network. Our study provides an outline for classifying large corporate social media feedback using LSTM networks and presents a methodology that can be expanded to accommodate an even broader range of product categories. Additionally, we make the code and dataset available to the scientific community for future use.

In this paper, we examine a specific non-linear electrodynamics model and explore the effects of an external Yang-Mills field on black hole physics. The model in question is a conformally invariant theory with a non-trivial impact on general relativity and electromagnetism, and we find that it leads to a change in shadow radius and a modification of the thermal Hawking flux from the black hole. The paper also outlines the methodology for extending these findings to the case of Yang-Mills fields with an arbitrary number of scalar fields. We further investigate the relationship between the shadow radius and the conformally invariant Yang-Mills charge parameter, and observe a direct, non-linear correlation between them. The results obtained can serve as a foundation for studying other metrics and spacetimes within the same category of conformally invariant theories. The paper's scope also extends to other research opportunities inspired by the same physical principles. The effectiveness of the conformal method is demonstrated by the simple yet exact solutions offered for the Reissner-Nordström black hole and its corresponding dyad vector. The paper's main contributions are made manifest through the development of an intuitive, visual representation of the Hawking temperature as it responds to the Yang-Mills field. The relationship between the entropy of the conformally invariant Reissner-Nordström black hole and the Yang-Mills field can be expressed through the Yangentropy formula, which is found to be associated with the trapping region of the conformally invariant metric. The paper also explores the connection between the shadow radius and the Yang-Mills field within the context of the Fuzzball proposal. The results obtained for the conformally invariant Reissner-Nordström black hole are compared to those of the standard Einstein-Maxwell theory. The paper further delves into the application of the same method to the case of Einstein-Maxwell-Dilaton gravity. The analysis provided reveals that the conformally invariant approach can be utilized as a means of extending the principles of fuzzball thinking to a wider range of metrics. The paper also outlines the conditions under which the conformally invariant approach can distinguish between the interior and exterior regions of the event horizon through the analysis of the Hawking radiation. The event horizon's ability to trap both the incoming particles and the scalar field is demonstrated through the study of the conformally invariant Reissner-Nordström black hole. We examine the evolution of optical tomograms under a parameterization that is both periodic and non-periodic. Our investigation focuses on a laser system where a Nicardis map represents the dynamics. We find that certain nonclassical phenomena such as entanglement variations correspond to specific periods of the map. Moreover, we illustrate how entanglement fluctuations are geographically distributed within the Hilbert space based on the Wigner function. These findings are applicable to actual laser systems, including the Nicardis map itself. We also show that a particular periodic rephasing leads to a restoration of initial entanglement levels. Furthermore, we propose a method to accelerate the recovery of entanglement through the periodic component of the Nicardis map. We demonstrate the validity of our approach using a realistic laser model. This research demonstrates how the Nicardis map impacts entanglement over time and provides insights into potential strategies for managing entanglement in optical systems. This knowledge can be applied to a variety of systems, including both atomic and semiconductor-based ones. We investigated the reflectance and Kerr rotation of a magnetophotonic crystal with aluminum wires on a silver substrate as it related to surface plasmon interference near a Rayleigh anomaly. The interference resulted in sharp minima in reflectance and peaks in Kerr rotation, exhibiting polarization dependence and sensitivity to the angle of incidence. The interference pattern shifted with an external magnetic field due to a change in wavelength caused by the magnetization of silver. The combination of surface plasmon interference, Rayleigh anomaly, and the 2D Bragg resonance led to the appearance of the magnetic field-dependent features at specific angles of incidence. As incidence increased towards the Brewster angle, surface plasmon interference dominated the reflectance, while near the Rayleigh anomaly, the interference mainly contributed to a shift in the 2D Bragg resonance. The resulting spectra were highly sensitive to the angle of incidence and exhibited angular dependence that could be utilized in angular selective switching. The research demonstrated that surface plasmon interference near a Rayleigh anomaly is an effective mechanism for magnetooptical data storage and processing. The appropriate angle of incidence is crucial for realizing large Kerr rotation and small reflectance. The study also highlighted the potential use of surface plasmon interference in Bragg stop filters and optical delay lines. To achieve this, we identify the key inputs that result in specific outputs and establish a connection between them, effectively creating a shortcut for the small model. To further improve performance, we've also developed two training agents that can be black-box or semi-black-box, depending on the level of access to the model. An analysis of $B$ meson decays into two neutral $K$ mesons is performed using 349 inverse femtobarns of data from proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. Decays of $B_s^0\to J/\psi\to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0\to K^0\to \pi^+\pi^-$ are examined through the $B_s^0\to J/\psi\phi\to J/\psi K^+K^-$ and $B^0\to K^0\to \pi^+\pi^* \to \rho^0\to \pi^+\pi^-$ channels. Branching fractions for these decays are calculated relative to the known value of $B^0$ meson decay rates. This study delves into the concurrency properties of MongoDB's data model, specifically across its various deployments. To achieve this, we adapt current Concurrency Properties Analysis (CPA) techniques to accommodate MongoDB's data management tools, namely WIREDTIGER, REPLICASET, and SHARDEDCLUSTER. Our analysis reveals that these deployments adhere to either Strong Isolation or Weak Isolation, depending on their configuration. To illustrate the practical implications of CPA on MongoDB, we present two scenarios: the first involves identifying the CPA of transactional deployments in MongoDB, while the second explores how CPA can be utilized to prevent deadlocks in MongoDB. Additionally, we outline potential future research directions for CPA, including how it can be applied to other NoSQL databases that incorporate distributed transactions. This investigation highlights the significance of Concurrency Properties Analysis in the context of MongoDB, while also highlighting the broader implications for the NoSQL community. To facilitate this research, our findings and approaches are made publicly available through an executable code repository on GitHub. This repository further enables the replication of our results and paves the way for an extension of our work to the vast majority of NoSQL databases that employ concurrency control mechanisms. This extension is feasible because the underlying principles of CPA are inherently portable. This research is an initial step towards a more comprehensive examination of CPA within the complex ecosystem of modern database systems, emphasizing the necessity to integrate CPA into testing frameworks and development environments, just as we currently ensure the integrity of database systems through tests for concurrency properties, snapshot isolation, and liveness in the presence of transactions. This research is an extension of our previous investigation into the CPA of Redis, another widely used NoSQL database. This earlier study discovered specific configurations of Redis that could lead to deadlocks and provided updates on the current state of Redis according to its developers. This earlier study was an analysis of the CPA of Redis based on its publicly available documentation, while the current study involves actual executions of MongoDB deployments. This research was an unexpected outcome of our efforts to ensure the integrity of MongoDB, following the discovery of possible deadlocks in its default configuration. This discovery led to an enhancement request to the MongoDB development community, which resulted in an update from the MongoDB developers on the CPA of their database system. A generation's socioeconomic status is greatly influenced by the opportunities allocated to it, which in turn affects future generations. This concept highlights the significance of social mobility within a society. A mathematical model is developed to analyze how opportunity allocation affects a society's overall well-being over time, taking into account factors like fairness, and it is applied to an example involving education systems. Additionally, we examine the relationship between fair opportunity allocation and generational mobility in a simulation using a random walk model. Furthermore, we discuss the limitations of the model given data constraints and possible policy implications. A similar model is also used to investigate the effects of education on social mobility in a society similar to that found in the United States. This model highlights the importance of considering intergenerational factors when analyzing social mobility and highlights the challenges faced in developing descriptive policy recommendations based on current data. This research emphasizes the value of integrating both short-term and long-term perspectives when evaluating opportunities within a society. This involves examining the chances that each member of the current population has of reaching certain socioeconomic milestones, in addition to studying the chances of future generations. This knowledge gap is addressed by developing mathematical models that incorporate both current and future socioeconomic conditions, which can be used to better understand the complex dynamics of social mobility. This research also explores possible policy interventions that can enhance opportunity allocation by prioritizing the most disadvantaged members of the population, which can be achieved through fair allocation methods, and by examining the effectiveness of these interventions on overall societal well-being, as well as the well-being of individual generations, based on a simulation using a random walk model. This paper addresses a critical issue in distributed optimization, where multiple agents collaborate to minimize a common cost function, including some agents that deliberately disrupt communication. To overcome this challenge, we develop two algorithms: the adaptive weighted mirror-descent method and the non-expansive feasibility-preserving algorithm. Both techniques successfully prevent malicious interference and ensure the convergence of the average cost function. To achieve this, the adaptive weighted mirror-descent method requires access to precise cost function gradients, whereas the non-expansive feasibility-preserving algorithm can accommodate arbitrary cost functions. To apply these methods, we divide the set of non-malicious agents into two groups: inner-loop agents that communicate directly and outer-loop agents that coordinate with each other. This approach enables us to overcome the difficulty of distinguishing between malicious and non-malicious agents. We evaluate the performance of these algorithms under various conditions and find that a majority of non-malicious agents are typically required to maintain communication effectiveness. We also highlight the limitations of these methods when the set of non-malicious agents is small or the communication time horizon is short. We illustrate the practical significance of these constraints by applying these methods to a critical problem in operation research: the multi-agent transportation problem. This problem requires cooperation between agents of different types, including non-malicious agents and those that disrupt communication, to minimize the overall cost. We validate this model using a simulation based on real data from the transportation system of the city of Madrid, Spain. This simulation shows that even a small number of non-malicious agents can successfully cooperate to minimize the overall cost, despite interference from agents that deliberately disrupt communication. We also compare this approach to two alternative methods: the centralized coordination of all agents and a self-organizing approach that does not distinguish between malicious and non-malicious agents. This comparison reveals that the former method results in the lowest overall cost, whereas the latter method yields the highest cost. We emphasize that our primary contribution is the development of algorithms that can cope with malicious interference during cooperation between agents of different types. We also emphasize the significance of considering communication time horizons in cooperation problems and the challenges they pose. We highlight the critical role of type identification in cooperation problems and present two approaches to solve this problem. We evaluate these approaches based on the accuracy of their predictions and the robustness of their parameter estimation. To expand the capabilities of these spaces, we developed a new concept of spaces where angles can be accurately defined for points of intersection with any number of surrounding branches, and we demonstrated that this generalization enables solution to various conformal mapping problems in metric spaces of infinite branch points. Additionally, we solved the conformal embeddability problem for a specific type of space - an infinite tree-like structure - where each branch point has an infinite number of branches, providing in the process a more comprehensive understanding of the relationship between angles and this specific type of space geometry. Moreover, we established the equivalence of our approach to metric spaces defined by graphs, to networks with both directed and undirected connections, and to the spaces encountered in studying the dynamics of brownian motion in metric spaces. Furthermore, we tackled the problem of determining if a space can be made conformal if we are given the option of removing certain points of intersection, and we established criteria based on the properties of the space that ensures such an option exists. Lastly, we expanded the concept of spaces with angle information to those where angles can change over time, and we utilized this development to solve a time-dependent version of the conformal embeddability problem, and to study the dynamics of brownian motion in metric spaces that are constantly changing. To address information loss caused by channel errors in quantum communication, erasure correction codes are a potential solution. These codes can be realized using tensor networks, which are composed of a single species of tensor implementing the code's logical operations. For such a code to be effective, the tensor network must adhere to specific constraints to prevent decoherence and ensure accuracy. In this study, we examine a specific class of codes utilizing trilinear structure, specifically the Haah's cubic code, and provide an alternative implementation that meets the required constraints while being more manageable than the original version. This revised version can correct up to $n-1$ erasure errors in a space of $n^3$ qubits. Additionally, the code's variables and logical qubits can be efficiently identified through a single application of a unitary operator, which also scales more efficiently than other similar codes. The development of this code was facilitated by a distinct perspective on Haah's construction method, one that is more directly related to the underlying geometric structure. The resulting code's architecture, characterized by a high degree of symmetry, facilitates a significant improvement in the number of qubits required for a given level of error correction, making it the most compact variant known so far. The research on this code also led to an understanding of the Haah's construction from a new geometric perspective, one that is more aligned with the underlying structure of the cubic code, which in turn revealed this code's enhanced symmetry as a feature of the 24-cell geometry. The resulting code can be properly described using the 24-cell geometric framework, which it is found to be associated with, unlike the point-face intersection description indicated in the original publication. The study's findings also highlight the potential applications of the 24-cell geometry in quantum communication, specifically in the correction of errors in qubit memories. To enhance these predictions, it's essential to analyze the performance of these models across different stages of the processes they're a part of.  This research presents a data model that combines process data with machine learning models, enabling efficient storage and computation to facilitate performance analysis.  To demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, we developed a solution for analyzing a supply chain management scenario using stochastic processes and artificial neural networks.  This solution was implemented using a data integration technique and a set of tailored operators in the GiST data storage system.  The results showed that model performance could be accurately forecasted and that the approach could be applied to more complex scenarios.  The research was funded by the Norwegian Research Council and involved collaboration with Ericsson and Telenor ASA.  The data model and solution were tested on a large data set containing over 10 million process instances and 1 million machine learning predictions.  The source code for this project is available on GitHub.  This work was published at the IEEE International Conference on Data Science and Advanced Analytics.  It received the Best Paper Award. Researchers analyzed a solar flare observation from the Solar Orbit Wide Field Camera, which captured both optical and far-ultraviolet spectra of the flare, as well as a surrounding quiet solar region. The data were integrated for about 90 minutes and show significant changes in emission from the flare and surrounding area; this included significant line broadening in hydrogen wavelengths and varying levels of optical and far-ultraviolet continuum. The analysis indicates that even the most intense flares fail to fully absorb photospheric light, and that continuum and line broadening are closely linked. The findings also show that hydrogen line broadening is more intense in the lower atmospheric layers, whereas the Doppler width in the far-ultraviolet continuum is wider in the upper atmospheric layers. The study concludes that combining spatial and temporal resolutions will be crucial for fully understanding flare evolution. Nonlinear dynamical systems are challenging to analyze using traditional methods, especially when looking at the behavior of multiple interacting modes. To overcome this, the Koopman operator framework can be utilized, and we have developed a method to incorporate delayed feedback control within this framework. This approach generates a sequence of Koopman operators, which forms a chain of subspaces that represent the dynamics of the original system. We have derived an integral equation that determines the Koopman operators and have then taken the time-delay as the small parameter to be zero in the equation. This process yields a singular perturbation equation that can be analyzed to obtain an operator representation of the original system. Ultimate boundedness of the system's states and the states of the delayed states system are proven using the operator representation. Furthermore, we have shown that the Koopman operators converge to a limit as the time delay approaches zero, and these limit operators satisfy the same equation that was derived without the time delay. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, we have applied it to a nonlinear system with multiple interacting modes that exhibit complex dynamics, and the results show that delayed feedback control can lead to the coexistence of multiple oscillations at specific frequency ratios, as well as the breakdown of these coexistences as the time delay approaches zero. Moreover, we have observed that the delayed feedback control can lead to the generation of chaotic dynamics in certain conditions, and we have obtained numerical results using the Koopman operator method that confirm these findings. Furthermore, we have developed a method to estimate the Lyapunov exponents from the Koopman operator spectrum, which demonstrates the utility of this approach in analyzing the complexity of delayed feedback systems. We have also applied this method to a specific system to investigate the relationship between the time delay, the system's parameters, the frequency ratios, and the levels of chaos they support. To summarize, this research has shown that delayed feedback control systems can support multiple interacting modes that exhibit complex dynamics, and we have developed the Koopman operator method to analyze these systems. This approach has been demonstrated to be a useful tool for the study of delayed feedback systems, which are ubiquitous in nature and technology. Moreover, we have found that the Koopman operator spectrum contains the information needed to determine the Lyapunov exponents of these systems, which is crucial in understanding their complexity. We have also developed a method to estimate the Koopman operator spectrum from data, which makes it possible to apply this approach to experimental data. Animal population studies often struggle with obtaining accurate and comprehensive data, which can be challenging to obtain, particularly when it comes to wild subjects. A promising technique called spatial capture-recapture (SCR) models has been developed to provide precise population density estimates by analyzing both observed and unobserved individuals within a study area. These models have already demonstrated their effectiveness in various settings but have limitations when dealing with situations where some individuals occupy specific roles that carry significant weight, such as leaders in social species like wolves. In such cases, traditional density estimates might be misleading because they fail to account for the limited presence of these influential individuals. We present a new extension of the SCR models that takes into consideration the social status of animals and provides a direct estimate of density, including both high-status and low-status individuals, based on the interaction between capture histories and locations. This new approach was put to the test using data on black howler monkeys in Mexico, where researchers observed a notable difference between dominant and subordinate individuals within a population. The results showed that the new SCR model accurately identified the social status of monkeys and provided a population density estimate of 7.9 individuals per square kilometer, with a notable distinction between those of higher and lower status. The findings of this study demonstrate the value of considering social status in capture-recapture analysis, which can be a crucial aspect in certain animal populations, and the versatility of SCR models to adapt to diverse research settings while maintaining their effectiveness. This algorithm leverages an advanced technique called inverse partial program synthesis, which involves reversing the normal program synthesis process and uses the original software as a guiding principle. When put to use on four distinct programs and various test cases, our research showed that our automated method can pinpoint precise code modifications to address each separate error, even in the presence of thousands of errors. We analyze the root systems of types A and D, focusing on the properties of the highest root in these systems. Our in-depth examination includes both the classical roots based on an n-dimensional vector space, as well as the extended root systems within the (n-1)-dimensional subspace, often referred to as the "hypersurface" root systems. In our study, we derive various formulas that describe the relationships between the highest root and other roots within its respective system. Furthermore, we outline the methods for constructing roots on a hypersurface and provide explicit formulae to describe such roots. Our work also involves the examination of configurations of roots on a sphere of radius √2, representing a combination of both the A_n and D_n root systems. In this case, we identify the center of the root system as the point equidistant from the tips of all roots. Our research on the A_n root system shows that all roots on a hypersurface through the center form a copy of the A_(n-1) root system. By contrast, the D_n root system on a sphere of radius √2 exhibits more complex structure, as there are multiple distinct hypersurfaces through the center, each containing all roots of a D_(n-1) system except for exactly two roots which lie on opposite sides of the center. Our work on the D_n root system also reveals the presence of two distinct sublattices within the root lattice, both of which are isomorphic to the D_(n-1) root system but differ in terms of their configuration around the center. Our research further includes the examination of the relationship between the root systems of types A and D, focusing on the inclusion of the A_m root system within the D_(m+1) root system. In this case, we determine the coordinates of the roots on a sphere of radius √2, revealing the exact pattern in which the A_m roots are arranged around the center of the D_(m+1) root system. Our study also involves the exploration of the relationship between the root systems of types B and D, including both the universal parent system D_n and the children systems B_n and A_n. In this context, our research reveals the presence of two distinct lines within the D_n root system: one that passes through the center and is composed of all the roots of the B_n system, and another that is made up of all the roots of the A_n system except for exactly one root which lies on the opposite side of the center. A randomized algorithm is proposed for estimating network size within a specific time frame in fully connected and tree-shaped networks. This algorithm requires only constant-message exchanges and achieves an almost exact size estimation, surpassing previous approaches that relied on square root proportional information exchange. A key contribution of this algorithm is its tailored design for networks consisting of a single tier or a hierarchy, unlike other randomized algorithms that can handle more complex network structures. A theoretical analysis of the algorithm's accuracy is provided, along with experimental results that compare it to other centralized and decentralized algorithms. Our findings demonstrate that this algorithm delivers the most accurate size estimations among its counterparts in various network settings. Moreover, the proposed algorithm can be applied to a wide range of applications, including frequency domain networks, distributed memory management, and citizen sensing platforms. Our code is available online for the benefit of the research community.

We introduce a new solution method for the Hamiltonian constraint in the context of 3+1 dimensional gravity, specifically for the case of Kantowski-Sachs type spacetimes. These spacetimes have a conformally flat nature, yet the Hamiltonian constraint formulation treats the conformal factor in a non-standard manner, compared to the conventional approach that results in a second-order differential equation. Instead, the Hamiltonian constraint yields a first-order equation following an operation that effectively inverts the conformal factor. We refer to this method as the direct approach. The resulting equation can be solved for the conformal factor, after which the other constraints can be resolved to find the spacetime variables. We have verified that the direct approach leads to a consistent solution for Kantowski-Sachs type spacetimes, and our scheme has been tested using both analytical and numerical methods. Furthermore, the scheme has been found to be highly efficient in obtaining exact solutions, and it has the added benefit of eliminating the generation of apparent horizon in certain scenarios. Additionally, the scheme successfully prevents the expansion factor from becoming negative, thereby preventing big rip singularities, as demonstrated in an example where the model parameters are set to those found in a specific scalar field configuration. We believe the direct approach presents a promising solution method for the Hamiltonian constraint that can be applied to a broader range of spacetime scenarios. We also highlight the limitations of the conventional approach and provide a detailed comparison with the direct method. The muon's magnetic anomaly, specifically the discrepancy between the J-Park and BNL measurements, remains unexplained and requires further investigation. To explore the potential underlying causes of this discrepancy, including the possibility of a dark sector interaction, we examine the future experimental opportunities needed to comprehend the phenomenon. A J-Park-only analysis of the data reveals a 3.8$\sigma$ anomaly in the muon mass, which we also propose studying at future experiments. To investigate the implications of these findings, we outline the parameters for future experiments, including a J-Park upgrade with a 7.5 TeV proton beam and a detector utilizing a 1.2 km magnetic lattice to study dark sector physics. This setup would allow us to probe the effective dark sector-luminosity parameter at the level of $10^{-20}$ GeV or, in the case of a compliant J-Park measurement, to verify the muon mass anomaly at the 5$\sigma$ confidence level. To achieve this, we propose constructing a new muon detection system at J-Park, utilizing an iron-scintillator electromagnetic calorimeter to identify muons in the 10 GeV range. This experiment would complement other dark matter searches and provide insights into the consistency of the J-Park measurement. In addition, we find that many of the proposed parameters for the future J-Park experiment are already adequate to reach the 5$\sigma$ confidence level required to confirm the muon mass anomaly, indicating that such an experiment is theoretically feasible with the current setup. We propose an open-data policy to facilitate reproducibility in the research community. In both groups, high-resolution grid recordings accurately identified the movement intentions encoded in cortical activity, with a high degree of precision even when comparing this method to the more commonly used electroencephalogram technique. Decoding movements from the same recordings using a machine learning tool called a functional neural decoder successfully predicted key aspects of physical activity, including balance, walking, and oral communication, in individuals post-stroke. These predictions aligned closely with those assessed clinically through traditional testing methods. As a result, researchers now suggest using electrocorticogram decoding in clinical settings to facilitate physical activity recovery in individuals with post-stroke cortical damage. Furthermore, the study highlights the potential advantages of using grid recordings to improve the accuracy of decoding movements from electroencephalogram signals. A subgraph in a group's switch diagram is called separating if it leads to a non-trivial split in the group's partition. We demonstrate that for a class of groups that include surface groups and 3d geometrically finite groups, every action on a tree results in the group's action being conjugate to a free action on a tree with respect to a specific subforest, where each forest edge corresponds to a separating subgraph. Additionally, we show that for surface groups and 3d geometrically finite groups, this subforest is infinite and contains separating subgraphs of arbitrarily large diameter. Furthermore, we prove that for surface groups and a subclass of 3d geometrically finite groups, the subforest is minimally infinite, implying that it contains the image of all outer automorphisms of the group. Graphs in real-world applications often evolve over time in response to changing connections and node relationships. Current graph neural network decoders are largely static and do not account for changes in graph structure, potentially leading to errors. To address this challenge, we present DECENNT, a dynamic graph neural network decoder designed to accurately decode evolving graphs. By representing each data point as a set of nodes with interconnected connections across multiple time steps, DECENNT achieves significant performance improvements over traditional approaches, surpassing current state-of-the-art methods in several applications by considerable margins. Experiments on these datasets show a 20-50% boost in accuracy when using DECENNT compared to alternative methods, demonstrating the efficacy of this approach. Moreover, DECENNT's performance can be further optimized by a related technique called multi-step decoding, offering additional performance gains. All the code required for this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ParsonHong/DECENNT.

Analyzing the movements of individuals within groups is a common task in data study, but separating biological movements from non-biological ones can be challenging, especially when data is limited. We've developed methods to identify biological movement patterns within data, even with under 100 data points, and these methods have been successfully applied to studying the behavior of cancer cells in imaging scans. We've also created a metric to measure the difference between these biological movement patterns and the surrounding, non-biological data, which we call the "biological signal strength". We've tested these methods on real data related to cancer and simulated data, and the results show they're effective in extracting biological movement patterns and measuring the difference between biological and non-biological areas. Furthermore, these methods have been published in the conference version of this work, which appeared in the 2023 Conference of the International Society for Medical Imaging Computing. We've made the code for these methods publicly available, which can be used to extract biological movement patterns from data, regardless of the field of study. In the context of relaxation-based methods for sparse coding and nested subgradient schemes, we develop the Nested Neumann algorithm, which achieves a faster convergence rate and a higher inception depth than current state-of-the-art methods. The algorithm's efficiency is measured by its inception depth, indicating the number of iterations before the objective function starts to increase. Through theoretical analysis, we show the Nested Neumann algorithm reaches a deeper inception depth than the Frustrum Neumann algorithm, which serves as the current threshold for scheme sparsity. We also provide the Nested Neumann algorithm's inception depth and convergence time analysis under specific condition sets. Furthermore, we demonstrate the Nested Neumann algorithm's performance on various simulation scenarios, including a comparison with the Frustrum Neumann algorithm, the Frustrum Neumann scheme, and the nested subgradient scheme, on different coding tasks. Quantum systems exhibiting Anderson localization or topological properties can be distinguished by examining the momentum space connectivity of the system's energy spectrum.  In 2018, a proposal to utilize X-ray edge jumps for detecting the topological characteristics of Anderson localized or topologically insulating systems through the modification of an external electric field was made.  However, the feasibility of this approach depends on the ability to accurately identify the topological 'hole' that forms in the momentum distribution of the electrons' momentum space, particularly when this 'hole' is tiny.  A proposed X-ray technique that incorporates ultrafast photography can effectively detect these momentary topological features, thus making it suitable for detecting even the most transient topological characteristics of systems with short localization times.  In such cases, other techniques such as those based on X-ray edge jumps or Bragg peaks may fall short, but this technique can complement them by incorporating an in-depth examination of the initial stages of interaction between the system and an external electric field.  This is particularly true for systems that exhibit self-interference patterns over multiple localization cycles, and that display both Anderson and topological characteristics that are not fixed in time.  A relevant example is provided by a chain of Rytov Bragg reflectors that are driven by an external electric field and that exhibit both time-dependent localization of optical fields within the lattice sites as well as the formation of 'holes' in the momentum distribution of these fields, even in the absence of an electric field.  The proposed X-ray technique can also be applied to a similar localization of optical fields in a Michelson interferometer, and that too in the presence of self-interference patterns in the lattice sites.  A theoretical model that incorporates both an external driving force as well as an appropriate average over time of the initial stages of interaction between the system and the X-ray light is developed, and the proposed technique is found to be highly sensitive, with the ability to detect even tiny topological features that arise in systems with short localization times. As a result, this technique is considered to be the most sensitive one that can detect both time-dependent localization of optical fields within the lattice sites as well as the formation of 'holes' in the momentum distribution of these fields. We envision our feedback control method as a crucial step towards creating more complex robotic systems that can hike and jump on varied terrain. Knowing the annealing gap, the difference between the quantum Hamiltonian and the classical cost function, is crucial for optimizing protocol parameters and comparing them to classical counterparts. This research develops a novel method for estimating the annealing gap using the coherent displacement operator, which has been employed in a variety of applications, including quantum simulation and error correction. The proposed technique is demonstrated using both random trap oscillator models and protein structure prediction tasks. It shows that the average annealing gap can be accurately determined even in complex landscapes, serving as a valuable tool for evaluating quantum annealing simulations and implementations. It is also worth noting that the average annealing gap can be an unreliable indicator for certain types of problems, such as the one mentioned above involving protein structure prediction. Therefore, it is essential to evaluate quantum annealing on a case-by-case basis. This work is an extension of previous research focused on error correction mechanisms, where the annealing gap was found to influence the occurrence of quantum fluctuations and, in turn, the success of quantum annealing. It has also been observed that the standard quantum annealing algorithm's performance varies significantly depending on the annealing schedule's alignment with the energy landscape's features, which the proposed annealing gap estimation can help with by providing a more precise measure, referred to as the effective annealing gap. This new metric can be used to assess the efficacy of quantum annealing algorithms and develop more efficient ones. We investigate a compass state's meterological capabilities when its components are subject to uncertainties. A state's number variance plays a crucial role in this capability, and we found it to be ${\sigma}^2=R^2/3$ for the given state. Furthermore, this variance determines the state's precision in estimating a specific parameter, such as damping, and we showed it to be $(\Delta\gamma)/\gamma$ times the state's variances in components. Consequently, a state with variances ${\sigma}_x^2$, ${\sigma}_y^2$, and ${\sigma}_z^2$ for its components will estimate a damping of $\gamma$ with a precision of $(\Delta\gamma)/\gamma = ( {\sigma}_x^2 + {\sigma}_y^2 + {\sigma}_z^2)/R^2$. This implies that a state with equal component variances, each set to $R^2/3$, will estimate a damping of $\gamma$ with a precision of $(\Delta\gamma)/\gamma = 3$, which is independent of $R$. This result can be generalized to any average variance. Our findings reveal that larger grains significantly impede the efficient cooling necessary for the formation of large planets in outer disks. This issue becomes even more critical as we considered the effects of multiple grain sizes, which further hinder the cooling process. Consequently, we believe that the conditions necessary for pebble accretion in outer disks might be more stringent than previously thought. Furthermore, we discovered that dust growth is likely hindered rather than promoted by heat transfer, and that the temperature gradient minimum required for pebble accretion exceeds 0.45 in turbulent disks. We also analyzed the cooling process in dust envelopes around YSOs using the 9.7 micron silica emission feature, which provided additional constraints on the cooling efficiency, particularly in the outer regions of disks. These results can be crucial for understanding the evolution of protoplanetary disks and the formation of planets within them. We also propose observing the 9.7 micron silica emission feature as an indicator of pebble accretion in outer disks. Our study further highlights the significance of considering the effects of dust thoroughly, especially in the context of pebble accretion, disk cooling, and the formation of planets in protoplanetary disks. Recent research on classification tasks, including image classification and text classification, has successfully created dynamic backdoor attacks that are activated by specific input modulations. However, implementing such attacks on tasks like sentiment analysis and product category classification has proven challenging. Current methods that activate classifications through frequency modulations or temporal manipulations are not effective for these types of tasks, forcing researchers to explore other options, such as activating classifications based on the order of input data, relying on static triggers that target specific classes, or using activation that varies by instance. This paper addresses these limitations by developing three types of dynamic backdoor attacks that can be applied to various classification tasks, including those that are class-specific or that target the order of input data, and demonstrates the effectiveness of these attacks across multiple tasks and datasets. Additionally, necessary precautions are outlined to prevent false positives in attack detection methods. The developed code is available online for the purpose of further research.

High-precision astrometric measurements at the nanoparsec level can be achieved with the help of space telescopes like Gaia, but these measurements vary significantly depending on the ecliptic latitude.  As a result, a systematic analysis was performed on a sample of 34,607 stars with low eccentricity, located close to the Sun and on nearly planar orbits, in order to investigate the relationship between ecliptic latitude and the shift in parallax.  The research revealed that the observed shift in parallax is directly proportional to the cosine of the ecliptic latitude, and can be better explained by a slight modification of the linear relation rather than the commonly accepted quadrature relationship.  Furthermore, a notable discrepancy was observed between observed and calculated shift in parallax values for certain stars with specific positions and distances from the Sun.  These findings have the potential to refine the understanding of the relationship between ecliptic latitude and the shift in parallax, and could also imply the presence of a small scale distance variation within the solar neighborhood.  The proposed modification to the linear relation could be valuable for the improvement of parallax estimation methods used in high precision astrometry.  The research has been based on data from the second Gaia data release and focuses on a specific population of stars that are minimally affected by other astrophysical phenomena, allowing for a precise examination of the ecliptic latitude's effect on parallax shift.  The findings have significant implications for future high precision astrometric measurements in space.  The proposed modification to the linear relation could also be applied to other parallax estimation methods, and the observed discrepancy in some star data sets could merit further investigation into possible distance variations within the solar neighborhood.  The research is relevant to fields such as astrometry, exoplanetary science and the study of the solar system's environment. To create a more informed and versatile question answering system, it's necessary to incorporate a wide range of knowledge. However, incorporating vast amounts of knowledge can lead to overfitting, a common issue in NLP systems. To address this challenge, we developed a method to gradually gather relevant knowledge in response to user input. This approach leverages context-specific knowledge by routing information toward contexts where the knowledge is valuable. To achieve this, we designed a neural knowledge base that utilizes graph attention mechanisms to determine the most relevant knowledge for each context. To apply this system to real-world scenarios, we created a data set with crowdsourced annotations to guide our training data. To evaluate the effectiveness of our system, we conducted experiments using the MSRA knowledge graph and WebPageTaboo data set, resulting in significant improvements over baseline systems in terms of accuracy and system entropy. Furthermore, we demonstrated the versatility of our system by incorporating additional knowledge into a pre-trained BERT model, which showed a substantial gain of 5.2% in F1 score compared to the baseline system. We have developed a method to calculate vibrational frequencies for the highest energy states of small molecular cations using multiconfiguration time-dependent Hartree theory. Previous attempts to create complete spectral models for small oxygen-containing cations have been challenging. Our approach has been successfully applied to these cations by combining theoretical frequency calculations with experimental data from various sources. We have specifically studied the vibrational frequencies of the $\mathrm{H_2O^+}$ and $\mathrm{CO_2^+}$ ions using this method. For $\mathrm{H_2O^+}$, we reconstructed the 0.5 eV range above the threshold for dissociation into $\mathrm{OH^+}+\mathrm{H^0}$, and we also examined the degrees of freedom that influence spectral feature shifts. Furthermore, we re-examined the degree to which rotation affects the vibrational stretching mode in $\mathrm{CO_2^+}$, and we found that it can be significant. Our results demonstrate that even in situations where electronic structure calculations face difficulties, it's still possible to create accurate models of vibrational spectra by combining experimental data with additional information. Our approach can be applied to a wide range of molecular ions and it enhances the understanding of how degree of freedom interactions influence spectral features. The proliferation of large-scale learning models requiring substantial communication resources due to extensive parameter updates is a significant challenge. This study introduces FedHamerm a new framework that leverages random walks to facilitate cooperation among nodes in network learning and addresses communication inefficiencies. To evaluate the effectiveness of this approach, FedHamerm is applied to the classification of graph-structured data using graph neural networks and complex healthcare diagnosis data using a random walk-based neural network. Our results show that FedHamerm surpasses fednern and federated learning in terms of performance and scalability. Moreover, FedHamerm is found to be superior in scenarios where node cooperation is difficult, such as in highly dispersed networks. This approach can be further generalized to accommodate various types of cooperative learning and is suitable for a wide range of applications involving complex data. Individuals engaging in criminal activity pose a significant challenge to public safety and welfare. A subset of offenders struggle with mental health issues, and our research aims to explore the potential benefits of providing them with mental health treatment while incarcerated, with a focus on reducing future crimes. We created an artificial neural network to make predictions about the effectiveness of various treatment approaches on future offenses, taking into consideration factors such as a offender's mental health condition, the length of their sentence, and their past criminal behavior. Through a computational experiment, our findings indicate that mental health treatment can lead to a significant decrease in future crimes, with an notable impact seen from therapy over medication treatment. Moreover, our research discovered an important phenomenon called the "dose response effect," where an increase in treatment intensity does not always lead to better outcomes, and in some cases may result in greater recidivism rates. We also found that limiting intensive treatment to offenders with more severe mental health issues, based on a psychological assessment known as the PCGS, can produce even better results. We demonstrated these findings to hold true across distinct versions of our network, and our research contributes to a broader discussion on the most efficient use of resources for reducing future crimes among offenders with mental health issues. Our approach and results are valuable for policy makers and correctional officers, providing them with an empirical tool to make data-driven decisions about prisoner treatment with lasting effects on public safety. Multi-class medical image segmentation poses an significant challenge, particularly when data is scarce. To tackle this challenge, we develop a novel semi-supervised learning approach, which combines graph-based regularization and convolutional neural networks. The proposed method involves training a shallow classifier on labeled images and using it to create a probability map for all data points. Unlabeled images are then classified based on this probability map, applied to graph regularization to prevent overfitting. The model has been successfully applied to 3D multi-class segmentation and 2D single-class segmentation, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods. The code for this project is available on GitHub. Notably, our approach can be viewed as a form of spectral normalization that does not require the computation of explicit normalization layers. We propose a novel graph neural network, which we call Geometric Message Passing Network (GMPN), to accurately identify local atomic arrangements within materials by utilizing a customized message passing function inspired by the success of geometric structure prediction networks. The GMPN model successfully replicates various challenging tasks, including those that test the ability to recognize atomic coordination and chemically active surface terminations. Furthermore, it demonstrates the ability to pre-train a general representation learning module for atomic configurations, which can be easily applied to a wide range of material science applications, including diffusion kinetics and battery functionality. The GMPN model's capabilities are compared to those of competing graph neural network architectures, revealing its unique ability to effectively incorporate the spatial configuration of atoms through the customized message passing function. Deep learning knowledge tracing models have consistently outperformed traditional approaches by achieving higher accuracy in predicting student performance. However, evaluating these models is complicated due to the lack of publicly available large datasets, which has led to concerns about their scalability. To address this challenge, our proposed model, CTKT, uses a dual-layer structure to capture both content and sequential knowledge tracing patterns by incorporating attention mechanisms and graph convolutional layers. CTKT exceeds the performance of current state-of-the-art models, surpassing their accuracy by up to 12.5%. When put to a larger dataset, our model also exhibits a significant performance increase of 13.6% over the current best model. To further validate our model's effectiveness, we conducted additional experiments using both large and synthetic datasets, and our model was ranked top in knowledge tracing tasks across more than half of the experimental settings. Our model was also found to be more robust than the competitors when varying important hyperparameter settings, such as model size and learning rate. Notably, our approach was able to successfully apply to a larger, previously untested dataset known as the A3 dataset, which consists of over 50 times more data points than the conventional MOOC knowledge graphs. On these datasets, our model consistently displayed superior performance over the current top models. We describe the development of veriT, a back-end challenger for multiple satisfiability (MTS) solvers used in proof checking, and present the proof format's evolution since our initial presentation at the PxTP workshop. veriT has participated in proof-checking competitions and consistently ranked high in both speed and accuracy. Our experience suggests that a clear and concise proof format is not a barrier to efficient proof checking, and that the main challenge lies within the underlying theorem-proving technology. To facilitate the transition to a proof economy, we are making the veriT solver and our proof repository, containing over 30,000 diverse proofs, publicly available through the Coq and SMTLib interfaces. Furthermore, we highlight the limitations of current verification tools in terms of the logical principles they are based on, and outline potential future developments, including the integration of veriT with verification tools based on first-order logic. Given the set-theoretic foundation of most mathematical proofs, we advocate for the use of a proof format that can be easily translated from the output of any automated theorem-prover, and present our own approach to dealing with the set-theoretic implicitness through type inference. We also examine the relationship between the consistency of veriT and the GÃdel incompleteness theorem. Lastly, we discuss various proof formats currently in use, highlighting both the benefits and drawbacks of each, before proposing our own verifiable Intermediate Representation (VIR) based on a simple, expression-based syntax that includes both equality and fixpoint operators. VIR has been designed to address the limitations of existing formats by accommodating the most fundamental logical rules while avoiding the added complexity of type inference. As an open-source project, veriT, along with VIR, is poised to contribute to the proof economy with a focus on set-theoretic logic based on intensional types. We have also developed a set of viral tests to ensure the solvers' and proof repository's integrity in the face of future developments. These tests, in turn, will help us identify any future proof format evolution needs. We are making all of our data and methods available to the community through the following repository: https://gitlab.com/veriT/veriT/-/tree/main/papers/PxTP2021. This paper introduces the FedBuff algorithm, a novel approach that enables scalable, private federated learning by utilizing brute force cryptography. FedBuff tackles data confidentiality issues by encrypting user data, and addresses scalability problems by reducing user participation in certain rounds. The algorithm's specifications allow it to support large datasets and diverse participant populations. This study proposes a method to adapt general-purpose embedding components (GECs) for specific tasks without starting from scratch. Our approach leverages a related task to fine-tune the GECs, which can then be applied to an unrelated task. We tested this adaptation method using BERT embedding components and tasks from the Glue benchmark. The results showed that our proposed method outperformed traditional multi-task transfer learning approaches. Specifically, our method achieved performance improvements of 0.37% in SST-2, 0.53% in MRPC, 0.83% in STS, 0.63% in TPC, and 1.43% in WNLI compared to the original GECs. Furthermore, our method performed similarly to fine-tuning the BERT embedding components from scratch, but required significantly less computational resources. The code for our proposed method has been made publicly available on GitHub. The proposed GEC adaptation method also demonstrated strong performance when applied to a large, complex dataset, achieving accuracy rates of 0.85% below the state-of-the-art baseline in both positive and negative sentiment classification scenarios. The method's efficacy was further validated by conducting user experience surveys among 500 participants in the Amazon Mechanical Turk platform, where our GEC adaptation approach was preferred over other transfer learning methods by 28% of the participants. The proposed method has been named "FastTask" and the authors encourage further research to enhance the method for more challenging tasks that require more fine-grained models. The term GEC in the context of this paper refers to pre-trained contextual embedding components based on the BERT architecture. The authors test the method on tasks ranging from sentiment analysis to text classification, but note that the approach may be applicable to other types of tasks as well. Notably, our results relative to a gold standard, which is equivalent to a perfect and costless cut-and-choose allocation, demonstrate that Round-Robin provides an approximation that is roughly speaking, within a factor of two in terms of fairness and a certain measure of data discard, as well as within a certain measure of data leakage from a certain number of samples. These results can be viewed as a variation of previous findings regarding the fairness guarantees of Round-Robin when there is only one sample available. We also explore the application of our findings to the problem of allocating multiple, independent, and identically distributed samples to multiple agents according to the preferences of these agents, to the greatest possible extent without violating certain privacy constraints that are analogous to standard leakage bounds. Despite this similarity, UGC 8839's HII region distribution differs significantly from these two galaxies in several other aspects. With a majority of its HII regions situated in the galaxy's outer regions, UGC 8839's HII region population exhibits a distinct 10-fold increase in radii when compared to its total galactic radius. Furthermore, the majority of UGC 8839's HII regions are isolated and are not grouped in the spiral arms as seen in other galaxies. We propose that the lack of inner HII regions in UGC 8839 could be attributed to the low metallicity of its gas, while other factors such as stellar clusters, lack of massive young stars, or interaction with a companion galaxy may also be contributing factors. Additionally, the unusual distribution of the HII regions in UGC 8839 could be the result of its low mass. Some T Tauri stars exhibit extreme and short-lived fluctuations in their
brightness, which has led researchers to question traditional disk evolution
theories. Classic T Tauri stars, having strong and persistent variations in
their luminosity, were thought to quickly transition to the lower-luminosity
Wolf-Rayet T Tauri stars, but a lack of observational evidence for this
stage has created a puzzle. We studied DR 21OL, a classic T Tauri star with an
exceptionally large and brief fluctuation in its brightness, using high-
resolution spectroscopy and found evidence for a massive accretion disk with
a small tidal streamer. Additionally, we detected a faint, narrow emission
line from a prominent He II transition, which has never been observed in any
T Tauri star. We believe this star's unique features are the result of a
close approach to a massive protostar, resulting in the formation of a
wide, non-axisymmetric disk with both a massive inner disk and a streamer
component, which we present as an explanation for the variable disk
evolution seen in some classic T Tauri stars. We also found that the
dissipation of this particular star's disk streamer, along with a decrease in
its accretion rate, led to a significant decrease in its optical brightness. 
We propose a revised disk evolution scenario for these stars, with some
classic T Tauri stars experiencing large fluctuations in their mass gain,
resulting in varied outcomes, including some that quickly transition to the
Wolf-Rayet T Tauri stage, unlike the non-variable T Tauri stars. We also
found that the presence of a streamer component in a classic T Tauri star is
a short-lived stage, with a duration of approximately 0.1 million years, and
we present evidence that these stars can also experience mass loss through
radiation-driven winds induced by the He II emission. Furthermore, we found
that the relationship between total luminosity and mass gain rate in these
stars holds for both variable and non-variable T Tauri stars, with a lower
limit of 0.01 solar masses per year for the former and 0.1 solar masses per
year for the latter. We also determined the masses of these stars, with DR
21OL having a mass of 0.46 solar masses and an initial mass of 1.5 to 3.5
solar

A notable aspect of V392 Persei is the presence of strong magnetic field indicators, suggesting the presence of a strong magnetic field in the white dwarf.  This is particularly interesting because mass transfer is likely facilitated through accretion disks rather than direct winds, as seen in systems like AE Aquilae and PW Vulpeculae.  As a result, V392 Persei may offer a unique perspective on how a nova that was triggered by a sudden release of energy instead of accretion still affects the binary system's accretion state.
