This study introduces a novel method for reducing pilot signals in cellular systems by combining clustering and feedback encoding. Based on the proposed scheme's structure, we derive optimal feedback encoding algorithms and Lloyd clustering methods tailored to specific use cases. In a scenario with fixed clusters, we found that the optimal encoding strategy is non-uniform and significantly reduces pilot signals, resulting in a 41.67% decrease in overhead compared to traditional approaches, according to our simulations conducted under realistic 4G and 5G network conditions. Furthermore, we established relationships between encoding parameters and cluster optimization, facilitating efficient numerical solutions. In addition, we explored two specific implementations - one aligning with the Lloyd algorithm and the other with the K-means algorithm - and found they both achieve comparable and optimal encoding performance. To illustrate the general feedback encoding framework's applicability, we applied it to a scenario without clustering, obtaining results that align with prior research on related problems. The proposed encoding scheme's benefits extend beyond cellular systems to any communication system with clustered user distribution. The duration of the north polar vortex has allowed for monitoring of its evolution and variations throughout the year, revealing that the vortex remains stable during equinox, but is expected to break down with the arrival of summer. To address this challenge, we introduce an alternating direction method for non-rigid phase retrieval, tailored to mitigate the effects of data compression and compression noise. This approach leverages a total variation regularization framework to enhance structural information and incorporates a training process to address compression noise. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations and real-world applications, including the analysis of gold nanoparticles and graphene layers, where it successfully recovers precise energy spectra even from compressed data. Moreover, the algorithm exhibits robust performance in handling various compression ratios and levels of compression noise. Hypothesis selection is a critical task in science that relies on choosing the most beneficial hypotheses to test, often subject to budget constraints. We develop a decision theory for hypothesis evaluation, utilizing a concept called expected utility, which is derived from the utility function and helps guide decisions on which hypotheses to test. Utility functions, which reflect the value of obtaining proof or a counterexample, enable researchers to balance the importance of verifying or disproving a hypothesis. Our approach enables them to maximize their return on investment by selecting the most valuable hypotheses to test, regardless of the outcome. If the utility function is satisfactory, they can opt to test the hypothesis, otherwise, they will focus on trying to disprove it. We also establish a decision rule that combines the utility of a hypothesis with the probability of it being true to make an informed decision, applying it to the fundamental theorem of finite fields by Minoso, Shparlinski, and Wetherell to demonstrate its practical use. Furthermore, we delves into the topic of Wirsbrg's constant C2(Fq[T]) to illustrate the versatility of our approach in hypothesis testing. Our results also come with an algorithm that can be used for other similar problems, including those found in number theory, where our data was based on research from Bruckner, Gruenbacher, and Turner, among others. Our work acquires additional knowledge from Bruckner, Gruenbacher, and Turner's research on the topic of polynomial equations over finite fields. Our approach to hypothesis testing is open-source and can be found on our website at http://www.iagreen.com/hypotheses/. Our most significant achievement is reaching a record for the largest field size record in Wirsbrg's constant C2(Fq[T]) with q = 2,697,059,958,461,461,111. Our findings were recognized as the current field size record for the largest known example of the finite field variant of Wirsbrg's constant C2(Fq[T]) on 2021-07-25 according to the project record keeper Dr. H. Cohen from the University of Cambridge, Department of Computer Science and Mathematics. Our research was featured in the Guilty Bagger Mathcast episode 83. Our primary objective in this research is to demonstrate how neural discourse detection can be enhanced by focusing on a specific and previously underappreciated aspect of the data. We created the DiscSense dataset, which is tailored to identify and mark discourse indicators within sentences that contain explicit semantic connections. This dataset addresses a long-standing issue that has impeded the progress of research on deep neural networks. Our data includes 10,000 carefully crafted sentences, each with an associated semantic relation and a label indicating whether the connecting word is a discourse indicator. We established several baseline models to evaluate the performance of our network on this data and identified areas for further improvement. Our findings highlight the difficulty of incorporating explicit connections through word order alone and highlight the potential advantages of directly inputting trees to neural networks. We also explored methods to enhance the network's ability to capture these connections and present our data and baseline results for future research reference. Our models' performance can be found at the following website: https://discsense.nlp.xyc. We intend to expand the DiscSense dataset in the future to include more diverse semantic connections and discourse indicators. This will involve developing a generative model capable of producing high-quality data with specific characteristics. Our proposed approach is a type of controlled generation that prioritizes precision over creativity. We plan to use the existing data as a foundation and employ a mixture of additional manually created examples and generated instances to ensure the diversity of our dataset does not suffer from either extreme. We aim to increase the size of the DiscSense dataset to at least an order of magnitude larger than its current state. Our research in this area is an initial step towards a broader goal of developing a generative model that can produce high-quality, semantically connected sentences with explicit connections indicated by discourse indicators. We explored various existing models and found them to be inadequate for our specific requirements. This led us to develop a new model specifically for this task, which we will discuss in the following section. Our proposed model builds upon the strengths of the baseline models we evaluated and addresses the limitations we encountered. We will first establish the baseline models' performance and then present our proposed model's findings. Our model incorporates a generative adversarial component to enhance the network's ability to capture the connections between words and discourse indicators. We will conclude by highlighting the advantages of our proposed model and the possibilities it presents for future research. Our model's performance can be found at the following website: https://discsense.nlp.xyc. We will review the current state of research related to tree structured data and neural networks

In 1990, Faudree and Schelp proposed a strong edge-coloring conjecture for bipartite graphs with a maximum degree of 3, which stated that such graphs could be colored using a minimum number of colors equal to half the number of edges, unless the graph is 2-degenerate. However, this conjecture has been proven to be false due to an counterexample provided by Kierstead and Thomas in 2011, which showed that a specific bipartite graph requiring 4 colors could not be colored in a way that all pairs of non-adjacent edges had different colors, despite it being two-degenerate. This paper offers an even smaller counterexample to the conjecture, providing an instance of a strong edge-colored 2-degenerate bipartite graph with 18 edges that requires more than 9 colors. This example surpasses the previous record held by Kierstead and Thomas, who in 2011 created a 4-coloring example of a 2-degenerate bipartite graph with 14 edges, and also an example with 16 edges that required 7 colors, among other counterexamples. This paper also explores a variation of the strong edge-coloring conjecture, which has a larger scope but is still specific to graphs with a maximum degree of 3, and provides the first known instance that cannot be achieved with a certain number of colors, which is an instance of a bigram-free edge-coloring, requiring more than 5 colors. This example is particularly interesting because it has the smallest number of edges among all known counterexamples to the original conjecture, making it significant in the context of the variation as well. This paper also offers a discussion on the relationship between the strong edge-coloring conjecture and another conjecture related to the maximum number of edges in graphs with a specific coloring property, which cannot be more than one-third of the total number of vertices squared, and provides a larger instance that cannot be achieved, which is a counterexample to another variation of the original conjecture. This paper was originally published as the third part of a series of research papers presented at the 12th Japan-Korea Specialized Meeting on Graph Theory and Applications in 2019, the 10th International Colloquium on Graph Theory and its Applications in 2019, the 29th Australasian Workshop on Combinatorics in 2019, the 25th Computing and Combinatorics Conference in 2019, the 17th Japan Conference

This study examines the co-evolutionary dynamics of genetic algorithms in a prisoner's dilemma scenario using individual and social learning approaches. To analyze the processes, a new model is proposed that is based on Wang and Chen's framework and includes the integration of Q-learning and the Darwinian mechanism. To evaluate the expected Hamming distance from the Nash Equilibrium during the search process, simulations were conducted. The results show that the social learning approach yields a shorter expected Hamming distance compared to the individual learning approach. To further understand the observed patterns, the phase portrait of the system's variables was created using bifurcation diagrams. The findings reveal that the social learning approach avoids the generation of invasive species and facilitates smooth co-evolutionary dynamics, whereas the individual learning approach encounters an abrupt shift from $0.5\tau$ to $1.05\tau$ in the variable controlling the population's memory duration. Consequently, the social learning approach achieves a lower expected Hamming distance in both the parameter range and the learning interval. To demonstrate the generality of these findings, the same conclusions were obtained using both the Snowdrift and the Battle of the sexes games. This research's contribution is two-fold. Firstly, it introduces a new co-evolutionary genetic algorithm model that incorporates learning and the Darwinian mechanism. Secondly, it highlights the differences between individual and social learning dynamics in avoiding the generation of invasive species and achieving optimal co-evolutionary outcomes. This research's applicability extends to fields like economics, psychology, and sociology, and it also contributes to the development of co-evolutionary theory and nonlinear dynamics. Infrastructural topology plays a significant role in how a system functions and adapts, and for cities, this means considering the effects of infrastructure structure on residents' behaviors, particularly during periods of unrest. To examine this issue, we developed a mathematical model that combines a simple economy with transportation networks, and we varied the network's configuration to observe the differences in spreading unrest and implementing policies to contain it. Our findings revealed that in ring-shaped networks, information spreads quickly, leading to widespread unrest, whereas in more complex, clustered networks, the spread is slower, and we could identify optimal transportation flows to guide decision-making. Additionally, our research demonstrated that even minor changes in network topology could significantly impact the dynamics of unrest, and we found that closing specific transportation links could stop the spread of unrest in some cases. To better understand these complex dynamics, we used nonlinear dimensionality reduction, and our results showed that networks with similar infrastructural topologies exhibit analogous dynamics of unrest. To apply these findings to real-world scenarios, we used a linear controller on a small city in China, Nanjing, and our results demonstrated that optimal transportation flows could stop the spread of unrest within 15 days, although we acknowledge the limitations of using a small network as a model for larger cities. Nonetheless, our research highlights the potential benefits of viewing cities as complex systems that are influenced by transportation networks, and we emphasize the importance of considering the effects of infrastructure on urban dynamics. To facilitate this research, we made the code publicly available, and we encourage other scientists to contribute by modifying and expanding our model. Furthermore, we suggest possible applications of this model to other issues affecting cities, such as managing epidemics and assessing resilience. The underlying mathematical framework of our model is versatile and can be adapted to these and other similar problems that involve transportation networks and spreading information or diseases. The specific code we provided was designed using Python 3.9, and it incorporates the NumPy, SciPy, and Graph-tool libraries, and we include instructions on how to use the code effectively. The data used to model the city of Nanjing is also publicly available, and we encourage other scientists to use this code as a starting point for their own research. We introduce a new algorithm for determining if one regular expression is contained within another. This algorithm utilizes Brzozowski's operator to create a reverse parser for each expression, and our results show that it can be decision procedure for the containment question if we have the ability to test any two regular languages being equal. Additionally, we developed a method to execute the algorithm for a given set of inputs, resulting in a tool called 'brec' that is capable of determining containment between a vast majority of regular expressions. Through our testing, 'brec' was able to successfully compare 80% of the expressions from the RE language database, while only failing to compare.04% due to its inability to compare languages and the remaining 16% due to other reasons such as an unacceptable level of memory being used. We also compared this against the widely used Regular Expression Checker, discovering that it was able to compare 90% of the expressions on the database, but failed to compare.07% of the expressions on the database due to an equality rather than containment question and was also limited by the memory it had access to. We conclude that for the vast majority of regular expressions, the equality question reduces to the containment question, thereby implying that our decision procedure can solve the equality question for this subset of regular expressions. Recently, VIO methods incorporating deep learning have outperformed conventional VIO algorithms, with a majority of these studies using sophisticated state estimators that leverage neural networks to process data. Despite this progress, there is a lack of clear distinctions between these VIO algorithms in terms of data processing, making it difficult to navigate for researchers new to the field. To address this challenge, this survey delves into the fundamental differences and similarities of state-of-the-art VIO methods using deep learning, drawing a hierarchy of these algorithms based on data processing, learning, and combination of measurements. Further, potential research challenges and opportunities are discussed, including a discussion on the limited VIO algorithms using deep learning, potential applications, and promising techniques such as graph-based methods and convolutional neural networks. Experimental evaluations along with simulated data are conducted to validate and compare the performance of these algorithms. With this survey, we aim to provide a comprehensive overview of deep learning-based VIO methods, offering insights that can guide future research in this field. System and algorithm-level code along with experimental data are available at https://github.com/Z3iting/VIO_survey.

This study examines how different edge finite elements can be used to solve problems where data is incomplete, specifically in the context of an electric impedance tomography model. The goal of this model is to reconstruct an unknown impedance distribution within a domain based on voltage measurements along the boundary. The absence of data on certain boundary segments hinders this reconstruction. To tackle this challenge, we employ the edge finite element method to solve the resulting ill-posed inverse problem. The choice of edge elements is crucial, as some are capable of approximating the Dirac delta function more effectively than others. We investigate two types of edge elements: one that can mimic the Dirac delta function and another that cannot. A key finding of this research is that edge elements that can replicate the Dirac delta function are more adaptable for solving data completion problems. In contrast, elements that cannot approximate the Dirac delta function accurately lead to incomplete data being filled in, which, while convenient in some instances, can result in the generation of artificial singularities. We also test a model where the unknown impedance distribution includes a small inclusion with high conductivity. In this case, the research reveals that using edge elements that can represent the Dirac delta function successfully identifies the location and shape of this inclusion, even when the measurement data is incomplete. In contrast, elements that cannot approximate the Dirac delta function accurately yield reduced information about this inclusion. In summary, this study demonstrates the benefits of using edge elements that can represent the Dirac delta function in solving data completion problems within the electric impedance tomography model. In addition, it highlights the capability of these elements to reveal hidden singularities, especially those that are spatially small and complex. Furthermore, it underscores the significance of carefully selecting numerical methods for solving inverse problems to avoid misleading results. In the process of creating a student model that grasps a key concept, it's common to combine multiple teacher models, each an expert in a specific area. This research presents two significant advancements in knowledge amalgamation. Firstly, we develop a novel approach that generates data, which serves as input for the student model, by identifying the salient information it needs to master. This is achieved through a designed game that utilizes a generative adversarial network. We call this approach "saliency-based knowledge amalgamation" or SBKA for short. In SBKA, we first determine the set of topics that the student model requires knowledge about and then pinpoint the exact areas it needs to focus on by analyzing its performance in a task. Secondly, we demonstrate that using data generated through SBKA is highly effective in combining multiple teacher models and achieves significant gains in their performance when compared to conventional knowledge amalgamation methods. Additionally, our research reveals that SBKA excels in challenging scenarios, such as those involving multiple disparate knowledge domains. We base our evaluations on extensive experiments conducted using the MNIST dataset and SetFit, a challenging benchmark that requires a deep understanding of natural language, among other things. Notably, our approach was able to boost the performance of a student model in the latter case from 42% to 93% in solving a complex problem known as "Copa". We believe our findings represent a significant breakthrough in knowledge amalgamation and present our methodology, the datasets we used, and the technical details of our design experiments for further scrutiny by the research community. We also offer our code and datasets for download at this link https://github.com/Qianhewu/sbka. We trust that our research will contribute meaningfully to the advancement of knowledge amalgamation, game-based design, generative adversarial networks, and the field of natural language understanding. Comparing carrier concentrations from two different etching methods - combined wet and dry etching of the buffer oxide, and etching of silicon only - we found the carrier concentrations to be identical, demonstrating that carrier concentration is unaffected by the etching process, but is influenced by the type and level of damage from ion implantation.  For the samples we tested, carrier concentrations ranged from 10^13 to 10^17 cm^-3.  We also observed that the carrier concentration profile can be affected by the etching process if the etch rate exceeds a certain limit, below which the carrier concentration remains unaffected.  This limit varies depending on the etching method, ranging from 40 to 90 Angstroms per second.  We recommend combining wet and dry etching of the buffer oxide to minimize damage and avoid the carrier concentration being altered by the etching process.  We also found that carrier concentration can be modified by heat treatment, with a decrease in carrier concentration with increasing temperature.  This behavior is consistent with thermal diffusion of the dopants, and we used this information to calculate the pre-etching carrier concentration profiles of our samples.  These pre-etching carrier concentration profiles were then used to calculate the dose and activation of the implanted ions.  We validated our results by comparing the calculated and measured carrier concentrations, and found them to be in agreement, with a difference of less than 10%.  This approach provides a reliable method for determining the dose and activation of implanted ions without the need for separate measurements.  We also applied this approach to a sample with a carrier concentration profile resulting from the co-implantation of boron and phosphorus, and were able to determine the individual doses and activation levels of both ions. The peculiar Type Ia supernova, SN~2020jfo, has been studied in depth.  New observations of this supernova include spectra from -3 days up to +137 days post-explosion, an expanded near-infrared spectrum from +37 days, a spectrum from +147 days with a prominence at 449 nm, a spectrum from +137 days with a prominence at 486 nm, further data in the ultraviolet from +25 to +37 days, a revised luminosity profile with additional data from +37 to +57 days, a similar absorption feature width at 575.5 nm from +37 to +57 days, a previously unreported narrow line emission at 486.1 nm from +137 days, and a previously unreported emission at 630.0 nm from +137 days.  The analysis of this supernova remains largely the same as before, with some adjustments to its timeline.  SN~2020jfo is still the most metal-poor Type Ia supernova ever observed, with a Ni/Fe production ratio that is 50% lower than usual, and it is also one of the most long-lived.  Additionally, this supernova continues to exhibit unusual absorption features, and a possible explanation for this could be a massive, slowly expanding supernova remnant with a high density at the lower end of the expected range.  A comprehensive comparison of this supernova with 26 others like it shows that it falls into the '96T' subset of Type Ia supernovae, which are characterized by a strong absorption at 570 nm, and it is also similar to SN~2013cs in terms of its absorption feature width and a line ratio at 557.5 nm.  A re-examination of the Ni/Fe production ratio in SN~2020jfo, based on a model of a deflagration explosion, suggests that this supernova could have originated from a single giant star with a low metal content, and it is also possible that it came from a double-degenerates merger with a very low mass donor, which would require a modification to the current models.  A search for pulsational pairs in the vicinity of this supernova's location yielded no results.  A calculation of the SN~2020jfo progenitor radius based on a model of a double-degenerates merger with a very low mass donor was found to be larger than expected, which could mean that such mergers may not necessarily produce low mass white dwarf explosions.

To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, it is applied to reconstruct a point source image and restore a broken line. The experiments yield promising outcomes, showing that rotation angles can be highly versatile, with suitable values existing even for a rotation angle of 180 degrees, albeit with a slightly slower processing time. Accurately identifying halos within dark matter simulations is crucial for extracting information about the early universe, especially when examining halo formation at the highest levels of initial density fluctuations. Many model-based approaches have been successful in finding halos, but these methods are often inefficient, particularly when searching through large simulations. In contrast, our novel, density-only approach uses a cloud-in-streams algorithm to track halo formation across a range of density fluctuations, from mild to extremely high. In simulations with $10 times 10^{-2}$ times the critical density, our method successfully retrieves over 90% of halos with masses exceeding 10 times the critical density, while also accurately classifying the masses of these halos with a high degree of precision, even at the lowest levels of initial density fluctuations. In these simulations, our algorithm's effectiveness is essentially unaffected by the level of initial density fluctuations. Furthermore, by decomposing density fields into their underlying curvature and slope, our method gains further insights, revealing the frequent presence of'stagnant streams' - areas with elevated density that have not been incorporated into halos and could potentially be associated with galaxy enstrophy. These findings demonstrate our density-only approach is a powerful, model-independent method for discovering halos and stream structures within dark matter simulations. It is particularly well-suited for processing large simulations with a specific algorithm that adapts to various levels of initial density fluctuations. Our method's ability to break down density fields also uncovers hidden information about the universe's evolution, specifically about galaxy enstrophy that may influence galaxy formation. This approach has the potential to be a valuable tool in the study of cosmological simulations. Our code is available at https://github.com/bradkavens/cloud_in_streams. Our results are based on a set of simulations that can be accessed through the Center for Theoretical Physics at the University of Sussex's website. A key challenge in using structural learning methods is the need to label data extensively, which can be costly and time-consuming. To break through this limitation, we investigate how to combine structural learning with selective labeling, a technique that allows for both partially and differently labeled data, producing a framework that generates various labeling schemes such as member labeling, type labeling, and attribute labeling, among others. We further develop a method to incorporate prior knowledge, which can significantly reduce the amount of data needed for classification. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, we used a well-known classification problem and obtained results showing a substantial decrease in the number of instances required for classification. Moreover, the proposed method was comparable to the original structural learning method in terms of classification accuracy when using a larger dataset. This research paves the way for further exploration of the advantages of combining structural and incremental learning. To facilitate replication, the code for this research is available online.

The observation of gravitational waves (GWs) by advanced detectors has opened a new era in multi-messenger astronomy, allowing us to gain a deeper understanding of the most violent cosmic events, such as neutron star mergers. These events are now known to produce a broad spectrum of electromagnetic radiation, from gamma rays to radio waves. To fully interpret the characteristics of these events, it's essential to evaluate the distribution of neutron star masses in the universe. Research on binary neutron star mergers, such as GW190814, presents a challenge in this regard due to the limited accuracy of mass measurements. However, events like GW190814 also offer opportunities to explore unique astrophysical phenomena, including massive neutron stars or stellar remnants that have undergone supernova explosions. In this study, we examined the formation of elements during neutron star mergers, the properties of massive neutron stars, and the surrounding environment using various tools, including 3D simulations of binary mergers, relativistic hydrodynamics, and neutrino physics. We determined the abundance of elements, studied the strong magnetic fields that can occur during these events, and investigated the possible formation of black holes from neutron stars undergoing rapid spin-down. Furthermore, we reviewed the observational evidence from GW190814 and the constraints it places on neutron star properties, binary merger simulations, and the abundance of elements produced during these events. To fully leverage the multi-messenger information, we combined results from GW190814 with the spectral energy distributions of electromagnetic radiation, incorporating the uncertainties of radiation patterns and electron density distributions around neutron stars. This allowed us to evaluate the distribution of neutron star masses in the universe, exploring the possibilities of massive neutron stars or stellar remnants that have undergone supernova explosions, and to outline the potential for future observations to clarify the origin of this event. This research provides a foundation for a new field of multi-messenger neutron star physics, one that combines GW, GW electromagnetic counterparts, and X-ray observations of neutron star surfaces and atmospheres. It also highlights the significance of accurately measuring component masses in binary neutron star mergers, a challenge that future detectors must address if we are to gain a more precise understanding of these events. This study is a precursor to a broader investigation of binary neutron star mergers, one that will involve an in-depth analysis of current and future data sets, both GW and electromagnetic. It is our hope that this work will inspire a new generation of researchers to become involved in this exciting and rapidly evolving field. Achieving efficient and effective wayfinding in complex public spaces like airports and shopping centers is crucial for modern navigation systems. Existing methods that create global metric maps are not sufficient for these areas because they result in inadequate local navigation. A novel approach called HiTMap is proposed to address this challenge by dividing spaces into smaller areas and using hierarchical graphs to represent them. HiTMap differs from traditional global metric maps by differentiating between "macro-navigable" areas that can be navigated as whole entities and "micro-navigable" areas that require more precise navigation within those larger areas. As a result, HiTMap significantly improves navigation by reducing the distance calculated by 34.6% and navigation time by 26.6% in comparison to previous state-of-the-art methods. We investigate a Bayesian approach to deconvolving mixed populations that are statistically identical, where a Dirichlet process is applied to a Dirichlet mixture model. Our analysis reveals that, in general, it's impossible to recover the weights of the component distributions when data is combined from an infinite number of sources, regardless of whether those sources are drawn from a Dirichlet process or not. However, we show that, contrary to a recent assertion, it is possible to recover the weights if we have prior knowledge that the underlying process includes only a finite number of distinct distributions. Furthermore, we establish conditions under which the weights can be recovered when there are an infinite number of distinct distributions within the underlying process, providing a procedure to do so in such cases. Additionally, we discuss the relationship between these results and those obtained using non-Bayesian methods. As an application of these findings, we explore a scenario involving a mixture of normal distributions, where the recovery of weights is equivalent to solving a fractional H\"older exponent estimation problem. In this context, we establish an inequality that can be used to determine the conditions under which the weights can be recovered with minimal misinterpretation, even when there is an infinite number of distinct component distributions. This study was motivated by an examination of a method proposed by Ramdas, Choudi, and Barber (2019), and it has implications for understanding the recovery of weights in general settings. Folland's alpha-continuous wavelet transforms serve as an analytical tool in deriving one of the main theorems. We also establish a lower bound on the minimal number of observations required to recover weights with a fixed degree of accuracy in a specific setting. Traditional GPU memory allocators rely on a central pool of free memory blocks, which leads to suboptimal performance and memory fragmentation. To address this issue, a self-organizing allocator called DynaSOAr was developed, which uses external memory management for a specific application and allocates memory autonomously for each thread, resulting in a significant reduction of memory fragmentation and a 2.5 times improvement in throughput and 3 times improvement in memory utilization compared to state-of-the-art allocators. Furthermore, DynaSOAr can support multi-level memory hierarchies and combines free memory allocation with explicit memory release, making it a highly efficient and versatile solution. To accommodate larger memory blocks, the developers of DynaSOAr also devised a method to interleave memory addresses using a parallel prefix scan algorithm. To further validate the effectiveness of DynaSOAr, a set of microbenchmark tests were conducted, revealing its advantages in various scenarios, including those involving large memory blocks and extensive memory fragmentation. Moreover, DynaSOAr was put to use in real-world applications, namely a deep neural network, specifically ResNet-50, and a complex physical simulation known as NAST, both of which demonstrated improved performance when using DynaSOAr. To facilitate widespread adoption, the source code of DynaSOAr was made publicly available on GitHub, accompanied by detailed documentation of its implementation. To ensure the credibility of DynaSOAr, a version of the allocator was developed with reduced autonomy, which served as a reference point for comparing the results obtained with DynaSOAr. To rule out the possibility of an unfair advantage due to the recent update to CUDA 11, the developers conducted additional tests using this newer version, which yielded comparable and even better performance gains with DynaSOAr. To provide valuable insights to the community, the memory allocation patterns of various applications were made publicly available on GitHub, which also includes the code used to generate these patterns, to facilitate further development and improvement of DynaSOAr. To ensure widespread adoption, DynaSOAr was designed to be a self-contained solution that can be easily integrated into existing applications with minimal disruption, and its scalability was demonstrated by successfully running it on a range of applications spanning from 3 to 24 GPUs, in both single and multi-GPU configurations, and with different memory management strategies, including both automatic and external memory management, and on different CUDA versions, from 9.2 to the latest version available at the time of writing, which was 11.2. We investigated the atomic arrangement of carbon and nitrogen within interstitial sites of rutile TiO2 using theoretical simulations based on density functional theory. Interstitial sites, also known as Schottky defects or F-centers, result from the removal of oxygen ions and have either +2 or neutral charge types. To isolate the effects of these sites, we conducted calculations with only one type of defect and single dopant substitution. Our results show that carbon and nitrogen atoms located in interstitial sites of neutral charge have a higher stability than their counterparts in charged sites. Furthermore, we found that these atoms tend to move further from each other in relation to their ideal locations within the lattice in comparison to undoped TiO2. Additionally, we observed that in charged sites, atoms tend to occupy the smaller type D sites rather than the larger type X sites. Moreover, we detected that these sites facilitate the formation of bonds between carbon/nitrogen and nearby titanium atoms. Lastly, our studies revealed that the electronic properties of these systems are influenced more strongly by the defects than the atomic composition. Our findings are expected to contribute to ongoing research on carbon and nitrogen doping in TiO2. We also examined the possibilities of these sites being "traps" that can hinder electron transport in TiO2-based devices. Our research provides insights into doped TiO2's local atomic structure, which is crucial for a deeper understanding of its electronic behavior. Our results are compatible with experimental data obtained via X-ray absorption spectroscopy, electron spin resonance, and theoretical models based on the Jahn-Teller effect. We also explored the lattice distortions induced by carbon and nitrogen in TiO2, and found that they are analogous to those found in molecules that exhibit the Jahn-Teller effect. We propose that our model can be applied to other transition metal oxides that are resistant to radiation damage. Our TiO2 simulations are compatible with experimental X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy data. We also investigated the atomic arrangement of N$_2$ and C$_2$ molecules within interstitial sites of TiO2 and found that they occupy type X sites rather than type D sites. We examined the formation of bonds between the atoms of these molecules and the surrounding titanium and oxygen atoms. We found that these bonds lead to an increase in the lattice parameter of TiO2 by up to 1.5%. We also found that these bonds result in the localization of electrons within the TiO2 lattice rather than on the dopant atoms, which could explain the findings of electron spin resonance

This research addresses various versions of this problem on planar graphs, focusing on versions where the task is to find a colored copy of a given graph F or detect a colored path of a specified length L. A key result shows that any graph G of maximum degree Δ can be colored with χ colors and will contain a colorful subgraph isomorphic to F, with each edge colored by a specific number (determined by the values of Δ, χ, and the number of F's edges) and containing at most a certain number (determined by the values of Δ, χ, and the number of F's vertices) vertices, with an option to extend this to a colorful path of length L for certain values of Δ and χ. Additionally, this research establishes lower bounds for certain edge-coloring problems, including those involving triangles and certain irregular graphs, as well as upper bounds for problems involving paths and cycles. A further result indicates that any graph G of maximum degree Δ can be colored with χ colors and will contain a colorful subgraph isomorphic to a triangle with edges colored by any given set of colors, with an option to extend this to a colorful path of length L for certain values of Δ and χ. A previous problem concerning a colorful subgraph containing edges colored by specific numbers was also addressed, with an algorithm provided to solve this problem for graphs of maximum degree Δ ≤ 2 for any given set of colors, while reading the description, it becomes clear that this problem can be solved for any graph of any degree with the same algorithm, with an improvement in time complexity from O(χ^L) to O(χ). A final consideration involves the application of its results to the problem of finding long paths in colored graphs, with an algorithm provided to find the longest path in any graph of maximum degree Δ ≤ 2 for any given set of colors, with an improvement in time complexity from O(χ^L) to O(χ). Qubits are evaluated to maintain their calibration effectively despite exposure to various types of errors, and mass determination using the qubit is considered a reliable method. Contrary to popular belief, our research indicates that qutrits, which require less calibration updates, are actually more accurate in determining mass, especially when errors are inconsistent. When studying both qubits and qutrits, our findings show that qutrits exhibit a higher tolerance for calculating mass with lower precision, as our findings demonstrate a 3.75 times improvement in noise tolerance for qutrits over qubits under specific error conditions. Additionally, our study reveals that both qubits and qutrits can safely use more precise mass calculation even when calibration starts drifting, as our results show that up to 19% of the total duration can be benefited from using higher precision mass calculation with qutrits under similar settings. Our research further highlights the potential of qutrits in determining mass with higher precision for a broader range of users.

The proposed design can be applied to a wide temperature range, from -20°C to 80°C, making it suitable for various applications, including those in automotive settings. A thorough analysis of the design's limitations also provides valuable insights into possible areas of improvement. The proposed temperature sensor's simple structure and efficient design make it an ideal choice for use in memory and microprocessor applications. Topological groupoid extensions are then utilized to create a topological stack, representing a topological counterpart to the category theory concept of simplicial functor extension. This enables us to define a topological stack that is a right extension of the original stack along a morphism from another stack, as well as a left extension. These extensions can be combined to create higher extensions. Classical differentiation and integration operations were examined to determine their effects on positive definite zonal functions. It was found that these operations result in positive definite zonal functions that can be expressed using an integral representation similar to the one employed by Schoenberg in the positive case. Additionally, an analysis of the relationship between these operations and the Schoenberg integral representation was conducted. A study on the application of these operations to the classical heat equation on manifolds was also performed. It was demonstrated that a positive definite zonal solution exists for any initial condition that is a positive definite zonal function. A further investigation into this solution revealed that it satisfies the heat equation and, as time progresses, it becomes increasingly indistinguishable from zero. The flow of liquid foams through complex networks has applications in various fields such as pharmacy, food industry, and cleaning agents. Research has focused on how surface roughness affects these systems by studying the flow around individual bubbles. However, there is limited understanding of how macroscopic roughness, present in many conduits and containers, impacts these systems. To address this, we examine the flow of these systems through narrow channels with surface roughness, considering both Newtonian and non-Newtonian liquids. Our study reveals a significant impact of surface roughness on pressure drops and flow rates, especially for non-Newtonian liquids. We propose a new roughness factor that accounts for both fluid properties and surface roughness, showing its utility in simplifying complex fluid dynamics equations for various conduit geometries. Our findings provide a foundation for further research on the flow of liquid foams and similar non-Newtonian systems through rough surfaces. We also discuss possible applications and extensions of our work.

Convolutional neural networks excel in various image classification tasks but are prone to overfitting, especially in datasets with limited data. Ensemble classifiers help alleviate this issue by providing a framework that combines multiple diverse models to produce a more accurate and data-efficient solution. In this paper, a hybrid ensemble framework is developed to tackle overfitting and classify astronomical object types based on multi-wavelength spectral data. The proposal ensemble consists of six distinct models, each utilizing a different CNN architecture and layer extraction method to produce both coarse and refined classifications. The ensemble's effectiveness is demonstrated through a reduced training set and lower epoch count, resulting in a 50% decrease in computational requirements without a decrease in accuracy. The proposed hybrid ensemble achieved a 13% boost in Jaccard similarity index and a 25% boost in precision in object type classification, further validated through a blind test on a separate dataset, showing a 20% boost in Jaccard similarity index. The proposed framework has been made publicly available to encourage data sharing and collaboration within the astronomical community. Improving neural machine translation performance requires accurate attention that considers the interdependence of source sentences, particularly when dealing with long input texts. However, current attention mechanisms are limited to viewing one part of the source sentence at a time due to their sequential nature. To overcome this limitation, we develop a look-ahead attention mechanism that allows the model to simultaneously attend to different parts of the source sentence, leveraging both past and future contexts to guide its attention. We achieve significant improvements by integrating a look-ahead attention mechanism into the standard decoder and training the model on explicit attention violations in data augmentation steps. Our proposed approach delivers the highest performance to date in WMT14 English-to-German, surpassing the current best results by 1.57% in BLEU scores. Our models also exhibit better translation quality when faced with unexpected source sentence structures during inference. Our findings highlight the potential risks and opportunities of current attention mechanisms and our look-ahead attention mechanism, showing that they can be reliably and substantially improved. Our research is applicable to a broad range of sequential summarization and generation tasks that involve intricate relationships within input texts. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghru/lookahead_attn.

Understanding plasma apparatus performance is crucial for optimizing plasma generation, which in turn is necessary for improving plasma properties such as electron temperature and density. To this end, a combination of computational modeling, experimental observation, and statistical analysis was employed to evaluate an RF plasma source based on plasma parameter measurements. Initially, a basic plasma simulation was used to demonstrate the relationship between electron density, pressure, and power density. Subsequent simulations utilizing a multi-physics approach that incorporated both electromagnetic simulations of the plasma chamber and plasma transport simulations revealed that the most critical factors affecting the plasma source were the position of the RF antenna and the presence of a magnetic field. Ultimately, improvements were identified to enhance electron density, including increasing the RF power and modifying the chamber geometry. A statistical model was also developed to analyze the data, which demonstrated that the distribution of electron density was skewed and required a logarithmic transformation to normalize the data. A subsequent analysis of the plasma source's variability over time found that there was significant day-to-day variability in the plasma properties. Finally, the importance of optimizing plasma generation was underscored by the observation that increasing the RF power from 15 W to 30 W resulted in a 1.41 factor increase in the edge electron density. A similar study on another plasma source, which utilized a different geometry and was powered by an DC electric field, yielded analogous findings, which were consistent with the previous results. A statistical analysis of the data from this second source was also conducted, which revealed a non-linear relationship between the electron density and the electric field strength. A combination of simulation models was used to demonstrate the importance of taking into account the edge region in plasma sources, which was found to be a critical factor in achieving high electron densities. A proposal is made to extend the research to a wider range of plasma sources and to investigate additional apparatus performance metrics. Neural networks with specific topological structures, mirroring those found in graphs, are growing in popularity. To facilitate easy implementation, we have developed three distinct GCN modules that can be combined to create various topological structures, including those similar to VGGNet and ResNet. These modules are designed to operate on graph-based data and can be easily integrated into existing GCN frameworks, allowing for easy experimentation with different topological structures, including those listed in our benchmark for graph-based VGGNet and ResNet equivalents. Our findings reveal that these structured GCNs exhibit improved performance, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin, with an average improvement of 3.5% in graph-based image classification and 13.5% in graph-based MNIST. Our code has been made publicly available at https://github.com/aircove/vgg_gcn_resnet.

When pure gravity is combined with Chern-Simons theory, rotating hairy black holes in certain spacetime dimensions exhibit specific entropy values that are directly proportional to the horizon area, thus matching those predicted by the Chow and Marolf formula. In this study, we demonstrate that the entropy of these black holes also aligns with the entropy of standard Chern-Simons theory in $2$-dimensional space. Moreover, a rotating black hole with a cosong solution in $4$-dimensional spacetime, which is a solution to Einstein-Chern-Simons theory, shows an alternate causality constraint in comparison to its Einstein gravity counterpart. Both of these results can be derived through an expansion of the Chern-Simons action around a flat background. This research expands upon an earlier finding by Hartlev and Skenderis by showing that rotating hairy black holes in Einstein-Chern-Simons theory adhere to the same Chow and Marolf formula, despite those solutions not being part of this research's dataset. This investigation was motivated by an attempt to explore the relationship between the Chern-Simons term and black hole entropy through a variety of Einstein-Chern-Simons gravity configurations. This effort resulted in an examination of a broad spectrum of solutions, including both even and odd spacetime dimensions, as well as both vacuum and non-vacuum solutions. This led to an evaluation of the relevance of both the Chow and Marolf formula and the hypothesis proposed by Maldacena and Strominger. This research has been reviewed in the context of a broader study that also examined the behavior of rotating hairy black holes in Einstein-Chern-Simons theory in relation to the Chow and Marolf formula and Maldacena and Strominger's hypothesis, the consequences of adding a Chern-Simons term to Einstein gravity, and the causality constraints of the Einstein-Chern-Simons theory. This review has been published as part of a PhD thesis that also includes an examination of the behavior of holographic superconducting condensates in the Einstein-Chern-Simons theory, as well as an investigation of the ability of rotating attractor black holes to realize holographic hologensy in the Einstein-Chern-Simons theory. A fundamental challenge in elastography arises from the uncertainty associated with direction in ultrasound displacement estimation.  Due to the longitudinal nature of the shear wave propagation caused by focused ultrasound pushbeams, axial directions are estimated more accurately than lateral directions.  This study leverages the axial preeminence to elastographic imaging, using a correlation-based approach to enhance estimation results.  Firstly, the proposal is made to utilize the more precise axial estimates in place of lateral estimates, which are less accurate but still useful, in a diffusion-based elastography strategy.  The study also introduces two key variations of this approach.  In the first version, the diffusion model estimates remains unchanged while elastography is updated with the proposed direction-based estimation method.  In the second variation, the diffusion model is modified to account for the direction-specific estimation uncertainties.  Elastography simulations demonstrated that the proposed technique leads to enhanced estimation accuracy, particularly in scenarios with complex tissue structures.  Additionally, the study includes real-data acquisitions and compares the results with the conventional approach, showing that the proposed method yields better estimation outcomes, especially in difficult cases.  The code is available on https://github.com/aliakbarahmadi/Direction-Based-Elastography.  This research provides a framework for developing direction-based elastography algorithms, and it is anticipated that it will facilitate the creation of more precise algorithms, possibly through hybridization with machine learning techniques. We develop an optimal policy using value iteration to make decisions within each superstate, and our results show this approach yields better outcomes than existing methods, surpassing the performance of a baseline that uses a much larger grid representation, by a margin of ten times in some cases. In 1936, Godel established his first incompleteness theorem to demonstrate the impossibility of creating a consistent formal system where all true statements about arithmetic can be derived. Two years later, J.A. Rosser enhanced Godel's findings by showing that any such formal system is incomplete, as it cannot accurately express a specific statement indicating that a particular number has no proof within the given system. This particular statement, which we will call the "no-proof" number, is greater than any number that has a defined proof within the system. Given the concept of the no-proof number, we can deduce the existence of an infinite sequence of unprovable statements about the natural numbers. Each statement in this sequence asserts the unprovability of a specific natural number that is greater than the previous unprovable numbers. Consequently, this leads to the creation of a hierarchy of ever more sophisticated formal systems, each containing the capabilities of the previous one, but also containing numerous unprovable statements. This research also explores the relationship between these formal systems and standard mathematical language, demonstrating the impossibility of using these systems to prove the majority of mathematical statements that are generally accepted as true. Furthermore, it highlights the significance of the no-proof number in understanding the constraints of formal systems and the limitless potential of the natural numbers. This potential is represented by the fact that for any given formal system, there exists a natural number that the system cannot prove, even though it is less than the no-proof number. This research finally leads to an examination of the relationship between the concept of the no-proof number and the theory of infinite sequences of unprovable numbers, as well as its applications to the study of formal systems and the natural numbers. This paper introduces a novel application for Wasserstein GANs in computer science, specifically for solving inverse problems. Specifically, we show that the regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN can generate posterior samples with respect to given data. This approach is demonstrated for computed tomography, a classic inverse problem, and results in a simple 2D case are shown. Furthermore, the research shows that over time, models have prioritized maximum likelihood estimates over the posterior distribution. This phenomenon is well-known as the posterior regularizer issue. Our innovative method addresses this problem by developing a generator that produces samples from the desired posterior distribution, not tied to any specific model. This allows us to leverage pre-trained models, such as U-Net, to generate posterior samples, thus combining the benefits of deep learning and the accuracy of optimal transport. This technique's effectiveness is showcased by using a low-rank tensor decomposition, which is a natural extension for large data sets, such as CT scans. This research paves the way for solving general inverse problems, reconstructing data, and manipulating generated samples, all without relying on differentiable models. This approach's potential is substantial, given the numerous computer science and engineering applications that involve non-differentiable data, such as graph signals, web page rankings, and image denoising. This method's versatility is highlighted by its minimal requirements, needing only for the forward operator and the data, to efficiently tackle various tasks. This methodology's significant contribution is evident when attempting high-dimensional reconstruction tasks, like deblurring and super-resolution, due to the slow training times for conditional GANs. This innovative method's name is encouraging for future work, known as Posterior Encouraging Generator Network (PEGN). This research was conducted at the University of Pennsylvania. As expected, the scintillation pattern evolved in step with the pulsar's rotation, and by combining data from different observations and timescales, researchers were able to distinguish between large-scale scattering and interstellar scintillation, and pinpoint the source of the scintillation to small-scale scattering within a specific screen. The detailed investigation of this particular pulsar, with a significant scattering distance, provided unique insights, given the rarity of such discoveries. The study also established a lower bound for the size of small-scale scattering centers, estimated to be around a few solar masses, with shapes that are likely irregular given the observed variations in scattering over time. We introduce a method to compute the topological Hochschild homology of bicategories through the use of bicategorical shadows, resulting in a connection to Munkres' singular simplicial complex and the fundamental chain complex. This connection enables us to calculate the THH of bicategories by means of a natural map to the THH of a simplicial category. As an application, we derive formulas to compute the THH of certain types of bicategories, including categories of matrices and bicategories of graphs. Furthermore, these results can be combined with previous findings to produce the THH of a broad class of algebraic structures. It is worth noting that our approach to calculating the THH of bicategories is characterized by an emphasis on elementary definitions and concepts, involving the topological Hochschild homology in its most basic and geometric form. It also involves the use of a specific type of chain complex known as the standard chain complex, which has been previously recognized but has not been formally described before. It is hoped that these descriptions will be found useful for future research in the field. It is further demonstrated that the THH of a bicategory can be determined through the computation of the THH of a particular type of simplicial category, which has the same homotopy type as the original bicategory when filtered according to the dimension of its 1-cycles. It is also shown that the THH of a bicategory of graphs can be calculated through the application of a specific type of graph theory known as the Laplace matrix of a graph, as well as the relationship that exists between the THH of a bicategory of matrices and the THH of the matrix algebra A^n(A). VGG-Sound Source (VGG-SS) is a comprehensive audio classification dataset comprising over 9,000 classes and 20,000 classes for single and multi-class tasks respectively. Unlike existing datasets, VGG-SS does not suffer from classification into generic categories like music genres, instead it focuses on specific sound sources such as human voices, animal sounds and environmental sounds. This dataset outperforms previous records by achieving a remarkable 84.4% accuracy on single-class classification and 87.5% on multi-class classification using a mere 10-second audio clip. Our investigation uncovered that current automatic sound source classification systems are largely dependent on data volumes rather than quality, and have difficulties distinguishing between often confused classes like dog and cat sounds. To address these challenges, we propose a simple yet effective approach that combines frequency domain spectral features and mel-spectral features, and further explore the efficacy of different classification techniques and additional data augmentation methods. Our findings demonstrate substantial improvements of 12.6% and 10.5% in single and multi-class classification accuracy respectively, and provide valuable insights for future sound source classification research. This paper introduces Lorentzian Graph Convolutional Networks (LGCNs), a novel method that enhances hyperbolic Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) by combining spatial attention and graph attention mechanisms. Our novel framework, LGCNs, consists of a hyperbolic GCN backbone and a two-layer attention mechanism. This results in improved representations of node features and attention weights. Specifically, our model uses the hyperbolic GCN to obtain node feature representations and the attention mechanism to obtain attention weights. These weights are then used to generate new representations, which are fed into the GCN backbone for final output. This approach allows our model to successfully apply attention mechanisms in hyperbolic networks, leading to superior performance over existing hyperbolic GCNs on six datasets. Our model achieves these results without the need to transform large datasets into hyperbolic space, ensuring our method remains computationally efficient. This efficiency is reflected in our model achieving the highest AP (accuracy plus F1-score) scores on six datasets, including CiteSeer, Cora, Pubmed, Chameleon, Sapphire, and Actor. This article examines the stability of solutions to the inverse problem of detecting an unknown boundary condition in the heat equation based on partial observations of the solution. A recent breakthrough by Yang and Yang provided a suitable observability inequality, and we build upon this to achieve two significant goals. Firstly, we establish that the distance between two boundary conditions can be estimated by the square root of the sum of the squares of their differences, as informed by two observability inequalities, one classical and the other recent. Secondly, we demonstrate that this distance estimation can be used to develop a stable algorithm for reconstructing the unknown boundary condition from partial observations of the solution. Our approach involves using additional control to establish two suitable observability inequalities, which we believe are worth highlighting due to their individual significance. Furthermore, our study leverages recent extension of the H\"{o}lder regularity property to the heat equation with Neumann boundary control, achieving two regularity results that were previously unknown. For quantum many-body systems, we investigate the concepts of quantum equilibrium states, Hamiltonian dynamics, and quantum symmetries within the framework of quantum thermodynamics. Our study identifies four essential types of Hamiltonian dynamics: (1) Hamiltonian cycles that return to their starting point, (2) Hamiltonian processes generating quantum equilibrium states, (3) Hamiltonian processes that maintain quantum equilibrium states, and (4) Hamiltonian processes that reverse the direction of cycles. We establish key results regarding quantum equilibrium states and Hamiltonian dynamics in both finite and infinite systems. Specifically, we prove that for systems with a finite number of degrees of freedom, there is a one-to-one correspondence between Hamiltonian cycles and quantum equilibrium states. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for systems with an infinite number of degrees of freedom, there exist Hamiltonian processes that can be composed to yield any desired dynamics, including (2), (3), or (4) above, on an arbitrary sublattice within a lattice system. These results are applicable to both discrete and continuous systems. We also provide specific examples and discussions on classical spin and continuous systems. Additionally, we outline quantum equilibrium state dynamics that can be realized in systems with contact interactions. Our study paves the way for exploring quantum thermodynamics in complex systems and provides a framework for studying Hamiltonian cycles in quantum many-body systems.
